UNIT.subject: Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration in real-life situations
• Determining velocity and acceleration in different situations
• Drawing displacement-time graphs of different situations
• Interpreting displacement-time graphs in different situations
• Drawing velocity-time graphs from given tables in different situations
• Interpreting velocity-time graphs in different situations
• Relative speed of two moving bodies in different situations
• Application of linear motion in real-life situations
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the terms distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration in real-life situations
b) determine velocity and acceleration in different situations
c) draw displacement-time graphs of different situations
d) interpret displacement-time graphs in different situations
e) draw velocity-time graphs from given tables in different situations
f) interpret velocity-time graphs in different situations
g) determine the relative speed of two moving bodies in different situations
h) apply linear motion in real-life situations
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical thinking and problem solving: learners analyse the overtaking video, compare motion quantities and justify conclusions from graphs and calculations.
• Communication and collaboration: learners discuss predictions in groups, explain their reasoning using correct terms and present graphs and models to peers.
• Digital literacy: learners use video observation and, where available, simulations or graphing tools to collect and represent motion data.
• Self-efficacy: learners build confidence by revising their motion model across lessons and solving increasingly challenging problems.
• Learning to learn: learners track their questions on the Driving Question Board and reflect on how their understanding has grown.
UNIT.values:
• Responsibility: learners observe road safety rules and take care of shared equipment during measurements.
• Integrity: learners record and report measured times and distances honestly, even when results differ from predictions.
• Respect: learners listen to and build on peers' ideas during group sensemaking.
• Unity: learners work cooperatively in groups to gather data and build shared models.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions and defining problems: learners generate questions about how one car overtakes another for the Driving Question Board.
• Developing and using models: learners build and revise a model of motion using graphs, tables and equations.
• Analyzing and interpreting data: learners read displacement-time and velocity-time graphs to determine speed, velocity and acceleration.
• Using mathematics and computational thinking: learners calculate velocity, acceleration and relative speed.
• Constructing explanations: learners use evidence to explain how and when an overtaking car passes another.
UNIT.pcis:
• Road safety education: learners relate speed, overtaking and stopping distances to safe driving on roads such as the Nairobi-Nakuru highway.
• Citizenship: learners consider responsible behaviour as road users, including drivers, cyclists and pedestrians.
• Safety and security: learners discuss speed limits and the risks of unsafe overtaking.
UNIT.careers:
• Pilot and air traffic controller: use velocity, relative speed and acceleration to manage flight paths.
• Automotive engineer and mechanic: design and test vehicles using acceleration and braking data.
• Traffic police officer / NTSA officer: apply speed and distance measurements to enforce road safety.
• Athletics coach: analyse runners' speed and acceleration, e.g. 800 m races by Kenyan athletes.
• Civil engineer: design roads, overtaking lanes and junctions using motion principles.
UNIT.focus: This unit uses a video of one car overtaking another on a Kenyan road to motivate the study of linear motion. Learners progress from defining distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration to drawing and interpreting displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, then to relative speed and real-life applications. Each lesson follows predict, observe, explain, Driving Question Board and model building phases, so learners keep revising one model of the overtaking event.
UNIT.phenomenon: Learners watch videos of vehicles travelling along a road, such as a matatu, a lorry and private cars on the Nairobi-Nakuru highway near Naivasha, and one clip in which a car overtakes another. Both vehicles are moving in the same direction, yet the overtaking car appears to move quickly past the slower one while the speedometers show speeds that both seem high. Learners notice that the car being overtaken looks as if it is moving slowly from the overtaking driver's point of view, and that the overtaking car must speed up, pass and then return to its lane before an oncoming vehicle arrives. This is puzzling: how can two vehicles that are both moving fast appear to move slowly relative to each other, how long does the overtaking take, how far do the cars travel, and how can we describe and predict the motion using numbers and graphs?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A matatu from Kisumu to Nairobi speeds up after leaving a stage, travels steadily on the highway and slows down to stop, so its speedometer reading changes throughout the trip.
• A Kenyan 800 m runner such as David Rudisha increases speed at the start, then maintains pace and sprints at the finish.
• A boda boda rider travels 3 km away from a shopping centre and then returns, ending close to the starting point although the distance travelled is 6 km.
• A Standard Gauge Railway train from Mombasa to Nairobi travels at nearly constant speed on a straight section of track.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use distance, time, speed, velocity and graphs to describe and predict how one car overtakes another on a Kenyan road?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do you determine the velocity of a moving body?
2. How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Phenomenon – learners watch videos of vehicles on a road and a car overtaking another, predict what happens, and generate questions for the Driving Question Board.
Lesson 2: Learners explain distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration using real-life examples such as a boda boda trip and a matatu journey.
Lesson 3: Learners determine velocity and acceleration in different situations, including a car speeding up to overtake.
Lesson 4: Learners draw displacement-time graphs of different situations, such as a stationary vehicle, a steady car and a returning cyclist.
Lesson 5: Learners interpret displacement-time graphs to find velocity, direction and when vehicles meet or are at rest.
Lesson 6: Learners draw velocity-time graphs from given tables of data for vehicles speeding up, moving steadily and slowing down.
Lesson 7: Learners interpret velocity-time graphs to find acceleration, deceleration and distance travelled from the area under the graph.
Lesson 8: Learners determine the relative speed of two bodies moving in the same direction and in opposite directions, explaining why the overtaken car looks slow.
Lesson 9: Learners apply linear motion to real-life situations, such as the time and distance needed to overtake safely on a highway.
Lesson 10: Learners complete and present their final model of the overtaking event, revisit the Driving Question Board and answer the driving question.

LESSONS.title: Phenomenon: Overtaking on the Naivasha Highway
LESSONS.aresKeywords: overtaking, speedometer, distance, time, speed, velocity, acceleration, relative motion, oncoming lorry, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon by having learners observe a car overtaking another on the Nairobi-Nakuru highway near Naivasha, predict how long and how far the overtake takes, notice what is puzzling, and generate questions for the Driving Question Board.
slo.knowledge: Learners describe in everyday words what they see in the clip: overtaken car A at 72 km/h, overtaking car B at 72 km/h at the start and then faster, an oncoming lorry L, and car B returning to its lane. They recognise that distance, time, speed, direction and change of speed are the ideas needed to describe the motion. No formulas are taught.
slo.skills: Asking questions (NGSS SEP 1): learners write testable questions about the overtake. Developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2): learners draw an initial sketch model of the overtake. Analyzing and interpreting data: learners record qualitative observations and make predictions from them. Communicating: learners share ideas in pairs and with the class.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about everyday motion on Kenyan roads; respect for others' ideas; willingness to make a prediction and revise it later; a safety-conscious attitude towards road use and overtaking.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD key inquiry questions to be answered over the unit: (1) How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? (2) How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body? In Lesson 1 learners only raise questions that point towards these.
slo.purposeInStoryline: This lesson launches the storyline. Learners meet the phenomenon and raise questions such as 'how long?', 'how far?', 'how fast?' and 'is it safe?'. These questions open the Driving Question Board and are returned to in Lessons 2 to 10. Lesson 2 builds on the DQB questions about 'how far' and 'how fast'.
slo.safetyNotes: Video is watched indoors or in a shaded classroom; no learner should go onto a real road for this lesson. Stress that the clip is a recorded manoeuvre and that real overtaking is dangerous. Learners must never imitate overtaking on bicycles, boda bodas or on foot near roads. Keep walkways clear when learners move to the DQB.

LESSONS.overview: Learners watch short clips of a matatu, a lorry and private cars on the Nairobi-Nakuru highway near Naivasha, filmed by Kiprono from the roadside. They then watch one clip in which Wanjiru in the white Subaru (overtaking car B) passes Mr Kamau's blue Toyota Axio (overtaken car A) while Mr Otieno's lorry (oncoming lorry L) approaches from Nakuru. Before and during the viewing, learners predict how long and how far the overtake will take and sketch what they think happens. Achieng, in the back seat of car B, sees both speedometers reading high, yet car A looks slow from car B. This puzzle is explored through a Notice-Wonder discussion. Learners write questions on sticky notes and build the first Driving Question Board. No formulas, split-time tables or computed values are given in this lesson; the focus is on observing, predicting, puzzling and questioning.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown only a still image of the Nairobi-Nakuru highway near Naivasha with car A (blue Toyota Axio), car B (white Subaru) just behind it and a lorry far ahead in the opposite lane. They are told that both cars are going about 72 km/h and that Wanjiru in car B will overtake car A. Individually, in their notebooks, they write: (1) a prediction of how long the overtake will take (in seconds: under 3, 3 to 5, 5 to 10, or more than 10); (2) a prediction of how far car B will travel while overtaking; (3) a quick sketch of the positions of A, B and the lorry at the start and the end. They compare with a partner and explain their reasoning using their own experience of travelling in matatus on Kenyan roads.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the still image and say: 'Both cars are moving at 72 km/h. Wanjiru wants to pass Mr Kamau safely. Before we watch anything, I want your best prediction.' Read the three prompts aloud. Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Say: 'There are no wrong predictions today; we will test them later.' Circulate and note 3 or 4 contrasting predictions. Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What do you think happens to the speed of car B?' Then cold-call 4 learners to share a prediction and one reason, and record the range of time predictions on the board as tally marks. Do NOT say which prediction is correct and do NOT show numbers beyond 72 km/h.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage) with Think-Pair-Share: writing a prediction before seeing evidence makes learners' prior ideas about speed, time and distance visible, so that later evidence can confirm or challenge them. Pairing lets learners rehearse reasoning in low-risk talk before sharing publicly.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) predictions that include a time and a distance, not just 'fast' or 'slow'; (b) sketches showing car B moving ahead of car A and returning to its lane; (c) sketches that include the oncoming lorry; (d) reasons that mention speeding up. Note on a checklist learners who write only 'it is fast' with no number. Common ideas to record: 'B must go much faster than 72 km/h'; 'the overtake takes about 2 seconds'; 'both cars travel the same distance'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners watch two sets of clips. Set 1 (about 3 minutes): vehicles travelling along the Nairobi-Nakuru highway near Naivasha, including a matatu, a lorry and private cars, filmed by Kiprono. Learners complete a Notice column in a two-column table (Notice | Wonder) by listing what they see. Set 2 (about 2 minutes, shown twice): the clip of car B overtaking car A while oncoming lorry L approaches. In the clip both cars show about 72 km/h at the start, then car B speeds up, passes car A and returns to its lane before the lorry arrives. Achieng's view from the back seat of car B shows both speedometers reading high, yet car A seems to move slowly relative to car B. Learners record qualitative observations only: who speeds up, who keeps steady speed, direction of each vehicle, the moment B pulls back into lane. They compare what they saw with their predictions.
framework.teacherMoves: Introduce: 'Kiprono stood at the roadside near Naivasha and filmed these vehicles. Watch like a scientist and write what you see, not what you think.' Play Set 1 once without commentary. Play Set 2 first with no pause, then say: 'Watch again. This time focus on the speedometers and on how car A looks from car B.' Pause at the start, when B is just behind A, when B is beside A, and when B pulls in; at each pause ask: 'What do you see right now?' and WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 5 learners, one for each pause. Say: 'Both cars show a high speed. Yet from Wanjiru's seat, Mr Kamau's car looks slow. Does that bother anyone?' Do NOT give any measured values, split times or formulas.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Notice-and-Wonder with a pause-and-probe video protocol: separating what learners notice (observation) from what they wonder (questions) trains evidence-based description, and pausing at key moments focuses attention on changes in speed and position that the later mathematics will describe. Repeated viewing builds a shared experience for the whole class.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) observations that distinguish the steady car A from car B that speeds up; (b) mention of direction, for example the lorry coming the opposite way; (c) use of everyday words 'speed up' and 'slow down' correctly; (d) learners checking their earlier predictions against the clip. Listen for the key puzzle being voiced: 'Both cars are fast, but A looks slow from B.' Note learners who record opinions ('Wanjiru drives badly') rather than observations.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners discuss the puzzle: how can two vehicles that are both moving fast appear to move slowly relative to each other? They also discuss how long the overtake took, how far the cars travelled, and what an oncoming lorry has to do with it. Each group uses everyday explanations and sketches (no formulas) to produce an Initial Explanation Poster with three parts: (1) what we think is happening to car A, car B and lorry L; (2) our best idea about why A looks slow from B; (3) what we do not yet know. Groups revise their original prediction if the clip changed their thinking, marking the change in a different colour. Groups do a short gallery walk to see other posters.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Talk to your group. Why does Mr Kamau's car look slow from Wanjiru's seat, when its speedometer is high?' Give 5 minutes for discussion and 5 minutes for the poster. Circulate with the prompts: 'What is car B doing that car A is not?' and 'Which vehicle is coming towards you, and does that change how fast it looks?' Do NOT confirm or correct ideas; say: 'We will test this idea with evidence in later lessons.' Run a 4-minute gallery walk. After it, WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then ask: 'What ideas did you see on more than one poster?' Cold-call 3 groups to share one idea and one unanswered question. Record shared ideas and disagreements on the board, such as 'B speeds up', 'A stays steady', 'the lorry makes it risky'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial Models with Gallery Walk: asking learners to commit to an explanatory sketch before they have the tools to explain exposes partial ideas and misconceptions and creates a need to know. Comparing posters shows that different explanations compete, which motivates the investigations that follow in the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) posters that include car A, car B and lorry L in correct relative positions and directions; (b) explanations that link speeding up of B to passing A; (c) any attempt to link relative position to time and distance; (d) honest 'what we do not know' statements such as 'how long it takes' or 'how far B travels'. Note misconceptions such as 'a faster speedometer means the car must look faster to everyone' or 'the lorry has no effect on the overtake'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write 2 or 3 questions on sticky notes about the overtake, in the form 'How...?', 'Why...?', 'How long...?', 'How far...?'. They place them around the Driving Question on the board: 'How can we use distance, time, speed, velocity and graphs to describe and predict how one car overtakes another on a Kenyan road?' In groups, they sort the notes into categories such as 'How far and how long', 'How fast', 'Looking from another car', 'Safety and the lorry', and 'Graphs and numbers'. Each group chooses one question it most wants to answer and explains why. Learners note that some questions link to the two KICD key inquiry questions: how to find velocity and how to find acceleration.
framework.teacherMoves: Place the Driving Question on a large chart and read it aloud. Say: 'What questions do you have that would help us answer this?' Give 4 minutes of silent writing, with the prompt: 'Think about what you would need to know to describe and predict the overtake.' Collect and group notes with learners' help, asking: 'Where does this one belong? Why?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which questions look like they need numbers? Which need graphs?' Cold-call 5 learners to read a question aloud and place it. Highlight any questions about 'how far', 'how long', 'how fast' and 'is it safe', and tell learners: 'We will begin with these next lesson.' Do NOT answer questions now; say: 'We will return to this board in every lesson and move notes when we can answer them.' Keep the DQB visible in the room.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: collecting and categorising learner-generated questions gives learners ownership of the learning path and a public record of what the class wants to figure out. Sorting questions into categories reveals which ideas (distance, time, speed, velocity, acceleration, graphs, relative motion) the class will need to build.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) questions that are specific and testable, for example 'How long does the overtake take?' rather than 'Why do cars go fast?'; (b) questions that mention measurable quantities such as time, distance or speed; (c) questions about relative view ('Why does A look slow from B?') and safety with the oncoming lorry; (d) learners placing notes in sensible categories and justifying them. Record the number of learners who contributed at least one question and note learners who need support with question-writing.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners create an Initial Model Sketch on a half page of paper or in their notebooks. It shows a straight road near Naivasha, car A, car B, lorry L, arrows for direction of motion (Nakuru direction for A and B, opposite direction for L), and labelled positions at the start, in the middle and at the end of the overtake. Next to each vehicle they write whether it is speeding up, steady or slowing down, using everyday words. They add 'What I think will matter' with a list of ideas (for example time, distance, speed, gap to the lorry). They mark one thing they are least sure about with a star. They keep the sketch in their notebooks to revise in later lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw the first version of your model of the overtake. It is meant to change as we learn more.' Show a simple example layout without data: a straight line for the road and three small boxes for A, B and L. Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before asking: 'What should you include so that someone else could understand your model?' Cold-call 3 learners to name one feature to include. Circulate for 5 minutes and ask: 'How does your model show that B speeds up but A does not?' and 'Where is the lorry at the end of the overtake?' Close with: 'Keep this model safe. In Lesson 2 we start with your questions about how far and how fast.' Remind learners that overtaking on real roads is dangerous and that they should always keep safe on roads. Do NOT introduce formulas or numbers beyond 72 km/h.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Progressive Model Building: an initial sketch model records current understanding in words and pictures, which can be revised later with graphs and calculations. Marking uncertainty with a star links the model to the DQB and creates a purpose for upcoming lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) models that show all three vehicles and the correct directions; (b) labels showing car B speeding up and car A steady; (c) a list of ideas that matter, with some that are measurable; (d) a starred area of uncertainty that connects to the DQB. Scan for learners whose sketch omits the lorry or shows both cars moving in opposite directions and follow up in Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners make predictions with numbers and reasons? Which prior ideas about speed, distance and time were most common? Did learners voice the puzzle that both speedometers are high while A looks slow from B? Which DQB questions came from learners rather than from you? Were any learners dominating while others stayed silent, and how did cold-calling help? Which questions about 'how far' and 'how fast' should open Lesson 2? Did learners stay safety-minded? Note any learners who need support with sketching or question-writing, and keep the predictions and sketches for comparison in Lesson 10.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe in the clips? Describe in your own words what car A (blue Toyota Axio), car B (white Subaru) and the oncoming lorry L were doing, and what happened when B returned to its lane.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we notice that puzzled us? Record how the speedometers looked, how car A looked from car B, and what questions we now want to answer about how long, how far and how fast.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: What is our first explanation? Write your best current idea for why car A looks slow from car B even though both speedometers are high, and why the oncoming lorry matters, and say what you still need to find out.

LESSONS.title: Distance, Displacement, Speed, Velocity and Acceleration: Describing Motion on Kenyan Roads
LESSONS.aresKeywords: distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, scalar, vector, constant velocity, uniform velocity, non-uniform velocity, positive acceleration, deceleration, overtaking car B, overtaken car A, oncoming lorry L

slo.purpose: Learners distinguish distance from displacement and speed from velocity, and describe acceleration as the rate of change of velocity (qualitatively, with units), using a boda boda trip, the Naivasha Express matatu, the cyclist Atieno and the overtaking on the Naivasha highway, so they can start answering the DQB questions about 'how far' and 'how fast'.
slo.knowledge: Distance is the total path length travelled (scalar, m or km). Displacement is the straight-line change in position with direction (vector, m or km). Speed = distance/time (scalar). Velocity = displacement/time (vector, with direction shown by sign; the positive direction is towards Nakuru). Velocity is uniform (constant) when speed and direction do not change and non-uniform when either changes. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time, measured in m/s^2. It is positive when an object speeds up, negative (deceleration) when it slows down, and zero when velocity is constant. Car A has constant velocity (20 m/s), car B accelerates (20 to 30 m/s), and the oncoming lorry L has constant velocity of -20 m/s.
slo.skills: Classifying quantities as scalar or vector; reading a motion story and finding distance and displacement; comparing speed and velocity; using sign to show direction; asking questions and defining problems; analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP); constructing explanations using evidence; communicating reasoning in pairs and whole class.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how vehicles move on Kenyan roads; precision in using scientific words; respect for others' reasoning during discussion; responsibility and safety awareness on the road; perseverance when a result looks surprising (displacement 0 after a 12 km ride).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? 2. How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body? (This lesson builds the meanings; calculations come in Lesson 3.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 left learners with DQB questions about 'how far' and 'how fast' and puzzling speedometers. This lesson gives the vocabulary and the distinctions needed to describe motion precisely. It sets up Lesson 3 (calculating velocity and acceleration) and the graph lessons.
slo.safetyNotes: Classroom walking activity: clear desks and bags from the walkway and walk at normal pace only. When discussing road scenes, stress that learners must never judge distances or overtake while cycling or riding. Use the real clip only for analysis, not to encourage risky behaviour.

LESSONS.overview: Learners start by predicting how far a boda boda rider Juma is from the Naivasha stage after a trip and whether distance and displacement are the same. They then gather evidence by walking out-and-back paths in the classroom and by analysing three Kenyan journeys: Juma's boda boda trip (4 km distance, 2 km displacement east), the Naivasha Express matatu (90 km in 1.5 h) and the cyclist Atieno (12 km distance, displacement 0). In the Explain phase they sort quantities into scalars and vectors, define speed, velocity and acceleration, and classify cars A, B and lorry L from the overtaking clip as constant velocity or accelerating. They add new questions and answers to the Driving Question Board and revise the initial model of the overtake with the new vocabulary. No acceleration calculations are done in this lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners recall the overtaking clip on the Nairobi-Nakuru highway near Naivasha and the DQB questions on 'how far' and 'how fast' from Lesson 1. They read the story of Juma the boda boda rider: he leaves the Naivasha stage, rides east to the market, then turns back west to the school. Individually they predict in their notebooks: (a) Is the total length he rode the same as how far he is from the stage at the end? (b) Is a speedometer reading the same as saying 'going 72 km/h towards Nakuru'? They draw a quick sketch of Juma's path and write a prediction with a reason. No numbers are given yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the DQB and read aloud two Lesson 1 questions about 'how far' and 'how fast'. Say: 'Yesterday we wondered how far and how fast. Today we will find out whether those words mean exactly what we think.' Read Juma's story slowly without numbers. Ask: 'Without calculating, is the length of the road Juma rode the same as how far he ends from the stage? Write your prediction and one reason.' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds of silent thinking before any talk. Then pair-share for 2 minutes. Cold-call 4 learners from different parts of the room and record predictions in two columns on the board ('Same' / 'Different'), without judging. Ask: 'Achieng in the back seat of car B reads 72 km/h on the speedometer. What does the speedometer not tell her?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Record ideas about direction.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas through Predict-Share (Predict-Observe-Explain). Writing a prediction with a reason before instruction exposes everyday meanings of 'distance' and 'speed' and creates a need for precise definitions. Recording both predictions publicly lets learners compare their ideas with evidence later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for (1) a written prediction with a reason, (2) a sketch of the path showing the turn-back, (3) any mention of direction. Look for the common misconception that 'distance and displacement are always equal' or that 'speed tells everything about motion'. Tally predictions on the board (Same / Different) to compare with the evidence later.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Station 1, Walk the Path (10 min): In groups of 4, learners mark a 'stage' line on the floor with chalk or tape and walk a path in the classroom: 3 m east, then 1 m back west (scaled-down version of Juma's trip, 1 km = 1 m). One learner walks, one measures the length of path walked (distance), one measures the straight line from start to end with direction (displacement), and one records. Station 2, Journey Data Cards (15 min): groups analyse three cards. Card 1: Juma leaves the Naivasha stage, goes 3 km east to the market in 10 min, then 1 km west to the school in 5 min more. Card 2: Naivasha Express matatu, Nairobi to Naivasha, road distance 90 km in 1.5 h. Card 3: Atieno cycles from home to the Lake Naivasha gate 6 km away and back home in 1 hour (12 km of cycling). For each card, learners fill a table with columns: total path length (distance), final position relative to start (displacement and direction), total time, and 'what does the number tell us / not tell us?' Expected: Juma distance 4 km, displacement 2 km east of the stage; matatu distance 90 km, 1.5 h; Atieno distance 12 km, displacement 0 km. Learners also note that the matatu's 90 km is the road length and mention that its direction is towards Naivasha (north-west from Nairobi).
framework.teacherMoves: Introduce stations: 'You are motion detectives. For each journey, find two different answers to the question: how far?' Circulate to Station 1 and ask: 'Show me with your hand the path you walked. Now show me the straight line from start to finish. Are they the same?' Use WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after each question. At Station 2 prompt: 'Atieno ends at her gate at home. Where is she compared with where she started? What does that say about her displacement?' If groups say '12 km', ask: 'Is that the path length or the change in position?' Pull groups together for 3 minutes: cold-call 3 groups to report their table for Juma, the matatu and Atieno. Ask: 'Why can Atieno cycle 12 km and still have displacement 0?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds. Revisit the Predict board: ask 2 learners to move any prediction they now want to change. Do NOT yet introduce formulas for acceleration.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative data analysis with structured tables (Analysing and Interpreting Data, NGSS SEP 4) combined with an embodied activity. Physically walking out-and-back links the abstract ideas of path length and change in position to learners' own movement, and then the same structure is found in familiar Kenyan journeys. The three-column comparison (what it tells / does not tell) makes the distinction between scalar and vector explicit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: (1) correctly record Juma's distance as 4 km and displacement as 2 km east of the stage; (2) record Atieno's displacement as 0 while her distance is 12 km; (3) give the matatu's distance as 90 km and time 1.5 h without inventing direction numbers. Observable indicators: learners trace the path with a finger and then draw a straight arrow from start to end. Note groups who confuse 'displacement' with 'total length' and prompt them with the Station 1 walk.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Learners use their data to build meanings. Step 1 (8 min): Using the three journeys, groups complete sentence frames: 'Distance is ... It has/does not have direction. Displacement is ... It has/does not have direction.' Step 2 (7 min): Speed and velocity. Using Juma's trip, learners discuss: speed uses distance, velocity uses displacement and direction. They note that the matatu's average speed is found from 90 km and 1.5 h (to be calculated formally in Lesson 3), and that Atieno's average velocity must be 0 because her displacement is 0, even though she was cycling. They agree the positive direction is towards Nakuru, so lorry L, heading to Naivasha, has a negative velocity. Step 3 (10 min): Acceleration and the overtaking clip. Learners get a card describing cars A, B and lorry L: A steady on the speedometer at 72 km/h, B speeding up from 72 km/h to 108 km/h, L steady at 72 km/h towards Naivasha. They classify each: constant velocity or accelerating? Which has positive acceleration? What happens to the velocity of B? They draw a 'velocity story' for each vehicle using arrows (length = size of velocity, direction = sign) and write one sentence defining acceleration as the rate of change of velocity with time, with unit m/s^2, and the meaning of positive, zero and negative acceleration. They also ask: does lorry L have acceleration? (No, its velocity does not change, but its velocity is negative.) They state that a vehicle driving round a bend at a steady speed would still be accelerating because its direction changes (non-uniform velocity), but that on this straight road that does not occur. No numerical acceleration calculations are done.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We have three words that sound alike: distance, speed, and velocity. Let us decide what makes them different.' Run a Think-Pair-Share on each step. Step 1: ask 5 cold-called learners to read their completed frames; record the class definitions on the board in two columns: Scalar (distance, speed) and Vector (displacement, velocity). Ask: 'What is missing from speed that velocity has?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Step 2: ask: 'If Achieng's speedometer says 72 km/h in car B, and lorry L also shows 72 km/h, do they have the same velocity? Why or why not?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Correct gently: lorry L velocity is -20 m/s because it travels towards Naivasha. Remind them 72 km/h = 20 m/s (quote the conversion only as a fact, calculation practice comes in Lesson 3). Step 3: show the A, B, L card. Ask: 'Whose velocity changes during the overtake?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. 'Who has acceleration? Who has zero?' Cold-call 4 learners. Introduce: 'Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes. Its unit is m/s^2.' Explain deceleration is negative acceleration. Say: 'We will calculate acceleration next lesson; today we only decide when it is positive, zero or negative.' If asked for numbers, reply: 'Hold that question for Lesson 3; write it on the DQB.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning and Sorting/Classifying (Constructing Explanations, NGSS SEP 6). Learners use the evidence from the journey cards to claim whether each quantity is scalar or vector and justify it with reasoning about direction. Classifying A, B and L ties the new vocabulary directly to the anchoring phenomenon, building the language needed to explain why B's speedometer changes while A's does not.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the sentence frames for: distance = total path length, no direction; displacement = straight-line change in position with direction. Listen for correct classification: A constant velocity, L constant velocity (negative), B accelerating (positive). Indicators of understanding: learner says Atieno's average velocity is 0 although her speed was not 0; learner uses 'negative' for the lorry because of direction, not because it is slow. Exit prompt on a slip: 'Give one example from the Naivasha highway of a scalar and a vector.' Look for misconceptions such as 'negative velocity means slowing down' and address them in the next phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners return to the DQB from Lesson 1. In pairs they sort the existing questions on 'how far' and 'how fast' into three groups: those they can now partly answer (e.g. 'Is distance the same as how far the car ends up?'), those that need calculations (e.g. 'How fast is B going compared with A?'), and those that need new tools such as graphs or timing. Each pair writes one new question on a sticky note that arose today, for example: 'How do we calculate acceleration of B?', 'How can we show Atieno's trip on a graph?', 'How long does the overtake take and how far do the cars go?' They place notes on the DQB and add a green dot to questions that now have a partial answer.
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the DQB: 'Which of our questions did today's evidence help us answer, even a little?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 pairs to move a question and explain why with evidence from Juma, the matatu or Atieno. Ask: 'What new question do you have about car B speeding up from 72 km/h?' Collect at least 6 new sticky notes. Link questions to future lessons: 'Calculating velocity and acceleration is coming in Lesson 3; graphs after that.' Ensure two KICD questions are visible on the board: 'How do you determine the velocity of a moving body?' and 'How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body?' and mark them as 'in progress: we know what they mean, not yet how to calculate'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding. Sorting questions by what is answered, what needs calculation and what needs graphs shows learners that science builds over several lessons and keeps the investigation purposeful and student-driven.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count how many pairs correctly place at least one question into 'partly answered' with a reason from today's evidence. Check new questions for quality: are they about measuring, calculating or predicting the overtake? Look for questions that show confusion about direction or acceleration, and plan to address them in Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners revise their initial model of the overtake from Lesson 1 (a labelled sketch of cars A, B and lorry L on the Naivasha road). They add: (1) an arrow for the positive direction towards Nakuru; (2) velocity arrows for A (constant, 72 km/h), B (getting longer as it speeds up from 72 km/h to 108 km/h), and L (pointing the opposite way, labelled negative); (3) a short note naming which vehicle has positive acceleration and which have zero acceleration; (4) a note that distance travelled by B is not the same thing as how far ahead of A it ends up. They write a two-sentence explanation: 'Car B is accelerating because ... Car A has constant velocity because ...'. They leave space for numbers to be added in later lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your Lesson 1 model. Use today's vocabulary to make it more precise.' Model one example on the board: draw arrows for A and L and ask: 'Which way should L's arrow point and why?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Circulate and ask each group: 'How does your model show that B is accelerating and A is not?' Cold-call 3 learners to share their explanation sentence. Ask: 'What can your model not tell us yet?' Expect: how long it takes, how far, the exact acceleration, and whether it is safe. Record these on the board as 'next steps'. Collect models for the final model in Lesson 10.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Developing and Using Models (NGSS SEP 2) with iterative revision. Adding velocity arrows and labelled directions to the Lesson 1 sketch turns everyday observations into a scientific representation and makes gaps in understanding visible, motivating the calculations and graphs in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check models for: (1) a direction convention with Nakuru as positive; (2) lorry L labelled with a negative velocity; (3) B shown with changing velocity and A with constant velocity; (4) correct use of the words distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration. Use a 3-point check: all four present (secure), two or three (developing), fewer (needs support).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still used 'distance' and 'displacement' as the same word after the Atieno example, and which example convinced them? Did learners separate 'negative velocity' (direction) from 'slowing down' (negative acceleration), especially for lorry L? Which DQB questions arose that signal readiness for calculations in Lesson 3, and which learners need more practice with the positive direction towards Nakuru? How effectively did the walking activity connect to the Kenyan journeys, and how could the time allocation be adjusted to give more discussion time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Juma's boda boda trip: 4 km distance but 2 km displacement east of the stage. Naivasha Express matatu: 90 km in 1.5 h. Cyclist Atieno: 12 km distance but displacement 0. In the overtaking clip, car A stays steady at 72 km/h, car B speeds up from 72 km/h to 108 km/h, and oncoming lorry L travels the opposite way.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Distance is total path length (scalar); displacement is straight-line change in position with direction (vector). Speed uses distance; velocity uses displacement and direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity in m/s^2: positive when speeding up, zero for constant velocity, negative (deceleration) when slowing down.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Car A has constant velocity so zero acceleration. Car B has positive acceleration because its velocity increases. Lorry L has constant negative velocity because it travels towards Naivasha, opposite to the positive direction towards Nakuru, and zero acceleration. A speedometer shows speed only, so velocity is needed to describe direction as well.

LESSONS.title: Calculating Velocity and Acceleration: How Fast, and How Quickly Does the Speed Change?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: velocity, displacement, acceleration, deceleration, uniform velocity, unit conversion, km/h to m/s, negative sign, direction, overtaking car B, overtaken car A, oncoming lorry L

slo.purpose: Learners calculate velocity using velocity = displacement/time and acceleration using a = (v - u)/t, converting km/h to m/s and using the negative sign for deceleration and for motion in the opposite direction, so that they can put real numbers on the overtaking car B, the overtaken car A and the oncoming lorry L.
slo.knowledge: Velocity = displacement / time (vector; sign shows direction, positive towards Nakuru). Acceleration a = (v - u)/t in m/s^2. Deceleration is negative acceleration. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6 and m/s to km/h by multiplying by 3.6 (72 km/h = 20 m/s, 108 km/h = 30 m/s). Zero acceleration means constant velocity.
slo.skills: Using mathematics and computational thinking (NGSS SEP 5): substituting into formulas, converting units and checking signs. Analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4): reading values from the clip data. Constructing explanations (SEP 6): explaining why A has zero acceleration and L has negative velocity. Communication and collaboration through pair and whole-class talk.
slo.attitudes: Learners show precision and care with units and signs, persevere with multi-step calculations, and appreciate that mathematics helps us judge real road situations such as overtaking safely.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? 2. How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 gave learners the definitions of distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration (qualitatively, with units). Lesson 3 turns those definitions into calculations using the anchor data: A 150 m in 7.5 s gives 20 m/s, B accelerates from 20 to 30 m/s in 5 s giving 2 m/s^2, and the lorry has velocity -20 m/s. These numbers are the evidence that later lessons use for graphs (Lessons 4-7), relative speed (Lesson 8) and the safety decision (Lesson 9).
slo.safetyNotes: Do not take learners to a roadside to measure real vehicles in this lesson. Use the video clip and data cards only. Keep the classroom aisles clear during pair-movement activities. If a short walking or trolley-timing demonstration is used, do it in the school compound away from any road.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting the numerical velocity of Car A and the acceleration of Car B from the Naivasha overtaking clip, then work through the anchor data to calculate A's velocity (150 m in 7.5 s = 20 m/s), convert speedometer readings (72 km/h = 20 m/s and 108 km/h = 30 m/s), calculate B's acceleration ((30 - 20)/5 = 2 m/s^2) and assign the lorry a velocity of -20 m/s because it travels towards Naivasha. They then apply the same methods to two supporting situations, the boda boda first leg (18 km/h) and the braking matatu (a = -2 m/s^2), before adding the new evidence to the DQB and the class model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the Naivasha overtaking clip (Wanjiru in white Subaru B overtaking Mr Kamau's blue Toyota Axio A, with Mr Otieno's lorry L coming towards them). On a prediction card they individually write: (a) the speed they think A is travelling, in m/s, if its speedometer reads 72 km/h; (b) whether B's speed changes by the same amount every second; (c) what sign (+ or -) they would give the lorry's velocity and why, if positive is towards Nakuru. They share predictions with a partner and place a coloured sticker on a class tally chart (e.g. A: 20 m/s, 72 m/s, 7.2 m/s, don't know).
framework.teacherMoves: Display the still frames of A, B and L with arrows showing direction (positive towards Nakuru). Say: 'Yesterday we separated distance from displacement and speed from velocity. Today we put numbers on them. Before I show you any numbers, write your best prediction. There are no wrong predictions yet.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Why might the lorry's velocity need a different sign from A's?' Cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) to share, and ask 2 of them: 'What made you choose that?' Record all ideas on the board without judging them. Close with: 'Keep your card. We will test these predictions with evidence from the clip.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with a tally chart. Committing to a written prediction exposes misconceptions (for example that 72 km/h equals 72 m/s, or that the lorry's velocity is positive because it is fast), so learners have a reason to look closely at the evidence and can later compare their old ideas with their new ones.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the prediction cards and tally chart. Look for: learners who write a number with a unit for A; learners who mention direction when discussing the lorry; learners who treat speed and velocity as different ideas (from Lesson 2). Note how many believe km/h and m/s are interchangeable, and how many think B's speed jumps suddenly rather than changing steadily. Use this to decide how long to spend on unit conversion.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners receive a data card from the clip (Car A: starts at the start point and travels 150 m in 7.5 s; Car B: speedometer 72 km/h at t = 0 and 108 km/h at t = 5 s; Lorry L: travels 150 m towards Naivasha in 7.5 s). Learners replay the clip segments or study the frames. Station 1: calculate A's velocity: 150 m / 7.5 s = 20 m/s towards Nakuru (+20 m/s); check this against the speedometer 72 km/h by dividing 72 by 3.6 = 20 m/s. Station 2: convert B's speedometer readings: 72 km/h / 3.6 = 20 m/s; 108 km/h / 3.6 = 30 m/s; then calculate a = (v - u)/t = (30 - 20)/5 = 2 m/s^2. Station 3: calculate the lorry's velocity: displacement 150 m towards Naivasha = -150 m, so v = -150/7.5 = -20 m/s (speed 20 m/s, velocity -20 m/s). Groups record the working in a table: quantity, formula, substitution, answer with unit and sign. Learners also use the split-time table to check B's velocity rises by 2 m/s every second (20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30) and that A's velocity stays 20 m/s at every time (zero acceleration).
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Ask: 'What is the displacement, and in which direction?' and 'Which unit must be in metres per second before you substitute?' Insist on units in every line of working. When a group gets 72 m/s for A, say: 'Does 72 m/s match the distance of 150 m in 7.5 s? Check it.' Do not give the answer; let the clip data correct them. At each station, WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after posing: 'Why does the lorry get a negative sign when its speed is the same as A's?' Cold-call 3 groups to report their station results. Ask one group to explain why A's acceleration is (20 - 20)/7.5 = 0 m/s^2. Prompt: 'Does zero acceleration mean zero velocity?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data analysis with a worked-calculation table (Using Mathematics, SEP 5). Using the same layout for each body (formula, substitution, answer with unit and sign) makes the structure of the method visible, and comparing A, B and L side by side builds the idea that velocity has direction and that acceleration measures change in velocity, not velocity itself.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners: (1) divide by 3.6 to convert km/h to m/s and can say why; (2) write units on every line; (3) give the lorry -20 m/s and not +20 m/s; (4) calculate B's acceleration as 2 m/s^2 using (v - u)/t, not as 30/5 = 6 or (30 + 20)/5; (5) recognise that A has zero acceleration yet a non-zero velocity. Record a tick or note for each group on the checklist.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners apply the methods to two new Kenyan situations and then explain their results in terms of the overtaking. Task 1 (boda boda Juma, Naivasha town): on the first leg Juma rides 3 km east in 10 min. Learners calculate velocity in km/min (0.3 km/min), convert to km/h (18 km/h east, +18 km/h) and then to m/s (18 / 3.6 = 5 m/s). Task 2 (braking matatu): the matatu slows from 20 m/s to 0 in 10 s. Learners calculate a = (0 - 20)/10 = -2 m/s^2 and write 'deceleration 2 m/s^2'. Learners then write a 3-4 sentence explanation, using the words velocity, acceleration, direction and sign, answering: 'How do the numbers 20 m/s, 2 m/s^2 and -20 m/s describe A, B and L in the overtaking clip?' They also answer: 'What would B's acceleration be if Wanjiru had taken 10 s instead of 5 s to reach 30 m/s?' ((30 - 20)/10 = 1 m/s^2, a gentler speed-up). Pairs swap explanations and give one piece of feedback.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Juma and the matatu use the same two formulas as the cars on the highway. Show me.' Pose: 'When the matatu slows down, why is its acceleration negative if its speed is still positive?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners. Press on reasoning: 'Say that again using the words change in velocity.' Address the misconception that negative acceleration means moving backwards: sketch the matatu moving towards Nakuru with a = -2 m/s^2. Ask: 'In what way is the lorry's negative velocity different from the matatu's negative acceleration?' Model one sentence stem: 'The velocity of ___ is ___ because ___.' Select two explanations to read aloud and ask the class to agree or add.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with pair peer feedback (Constructing Explanations, SEP 6). Learners must support each claim about a vehicle with a calculation and a reason about direction or change in velocity. Transferring the method to the boda boda and matatu shows that the formulas work for any straight-line motion, and contrasting negative velocity (direction) with negative acceleration (slowing down) addresses a common confusion.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect the written explanations. Success indicators: correct values (18 km/h = 5 m/s; a = -2 m/s^2; 20, 2, -20); the word 'deceleration' used correctly; direction linked to sign; B's acceleration described as the change in velocity per second. Flag learners who write acceleration = 30 m/s or who say the lorry is 'slower' because its velocity is negative. Give an exit ticket: 'Convert 54 km/h to m/s and find the acceleration of a car going from 0 to 15 m/s in 5 s.' (15 m/s; 3 m/s^2.)

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class DQB from Lesson 1 (questions about 'how far' and 'how fast'). In groups they sort the questions into: answered today (e.g. 'How fast is A really going?' answered: 20 m/s; 'Is B's speed changing steadily?' answered: yes, a = 2 m/s^2), partly answered, and still open (e.g. 'How far do the cars travel?', 'Why does A look slow from B?', 'Is it safe with the lorry coming?'). They add new questions on sticky notes such as 'Can a graph show the acceleration?' and 'What does A look like from B's seat?', and link each to the driving question about describing and predicting the overtaking.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. Which questions did today's evidence help with? Which ones need new evidence?' Hand each group 2 coloured stickies: green for answered, yellow for new. WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which question do you think we should answer next, and why?' Cold-call 3 groups to place a note and justify it by pointing to evidence. Highlight that the next lessons will use graphs (Lessons 4-7) to show these same numbers, and that relative speed will come later. Do not answer the open questions; add them to the 'Coming up' column.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board sorting. Sorting questions by whether evidence has answered them makes learning visible, lets learners see progress towards the driving question and gives them ownership of what to investigate next.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that sorted questions are placed accurately (for example 'What is the velocity of A?' is marked answered, 'How long does overtaking take?' is not yet). Note whether new questions refer to graphs, distance covered or relative viewpoint, showing that learners are connecting to the next lessons. Look for learners who can link a question to specific evidence from today.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add to their personal overtaking model (a labelled road diagram of A, B and L from earlier lessons). For each vehicle they add a velocity arrow with a sign and label: A: +20 m/s (72 km/h), zero acceleration; B: +20 m/s rising to +30 m/s (108 km/h), a = 2 m/s^2 for 5 s, then 30 m/s steady; L: -20 m/s (72 km/h towards Naivasha). They also write the two formulas, velocity = displacement/time and a = (v - u)/t, in a 'Tools box' beside the model along with the conversion rule 'km/h / 3.6 = m/s'. Finally, learners complete the sentence: 'Our model now explains ___ but cannot yet explain ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model should now have numbers and directions, not just pictures. Add the new evidence and mark what you have changed since Lesson 2.' Circulate and ask: 'Where does the sign of the lorry show in your model?' and 'Where on your model does B's acceleration begin and end?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to read their gaps sentence. Record common gaps (how far each car travels, how long the overtake lasts, why A looks slow from B) on the board, saying: 'These are exactly what the next lessons will answer.' Collect the models for review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with a 'what it explains / what it cannot yet explain' statement. Updating the model with quantities makes learners connect each number to a physical feature of the overtaking, and naming its limits keeps the investigation going.
framework.formativeAssessment: Review models for: correct values and signs (+20, +20 to +30, -20 m/s); acceleration 2 m/s^2 marked only on B during the speeding-up; zero acceleration for A and L; formulas and conversion rule stated correctly. Gaps statements should refer to distance, time or relative viewpoint. Provide feedback for learners who give B a constant 30 m/s throughout or mark the lorry as positive.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Which learners confused speed with velocity or treated negative acceleration as moving backwards? Did learners use the 3.6 conversion with understanding, or only by memory? Did the clip data (150 m in 7.5 s giving 20 m/s matching 72 km/h) help learners correct their own predictions? Which cold-called learners struggled to explain the sign of the lorry's velocity and need a follow-up? What changes to pacing or grouping are needed before Lesson 4, when learners start drawing graphs of these quantities?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that Car A covers 150 m in 7.5 s, Car B's speedometer rises from 72 km/h to 108 km/h in 5 s and that the oncoming lorry L moves towards Naivasha. We observed that the matatu slows from 20 m/s to 0 in 10 s.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that velocity = displacement/time and a = (v - u)/t, that km/h is converted to m/s by dividing by 3.6, and that a negative sign shows direction (the lorry, -20 m/s) or deceleration (the braking matatu, a = -2 m/s^2).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that A has velocity +20 m/s with zero acceleration, B has acceleration 2 m/s^2 while it speeds up from 20 to 30 m/s, and L has velocity -20 m/s because it travels in the opposite direction, so the numbers describe how each vehicle moves in the overtaking.

LESSONS.title: Drawing Displacement-Time Graphs: Parked, Steady and Returning Movements
LESSONS.aresKeywords: displacement-time graph, scale, axes, plotting, horizontal line, straight line, returning movement, parked matatu, steady car, cyclist Atieno, Naivasha

slo.purpose: Learners choose suitable scales, plot points and draw straight-line displacement-time graphs for a stationary vehicle, a steady car and a returning cyclist, and describe the shape of each graph. This gives them the graph-drawing skill they will later use to describe the overtaking on the Naivasha highway.
slo.knowledge: Learners know that a displacement-time graph has time t on the x-axis and displacement on the y-axis. They know that a parked vehicle gives a horizontal line, a steady car gives a straight sloping line, and a returning movement rises, stays flat and then falls back to zero. They recall from Lessons 2-3 that displacement is a vector with direction and that velocity = displacement/time.
slo.skills: Choosing scales to fit a data table onto graph paper; labelling axes with quantity and unit; plotting points accurately; joining points with a ruler; describing the shape of a graph in words (Science and Engineering Practice: developing and using models; analysing data).
slo.attitudes: Learners show accuracy, neatness and perseverance when drawing graphs, and value careful checking and peer feedback.
slo.keyInquiry: How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? (This lesson prepares the graphs from which velocity will be read in Lesson 5.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 2-3 gave learners the ideas of displacement and velocity = displacement/time. Lesson 4 turns movement into pictures. Learners draw three displacement-time graphs (parked matatu, steady car, returning cyclist Atieno) so that in Lesson 5 they can interpret them. The graph shapes are also a first step toward describing Car A's steady motion and Car B's changing motion in the overtaking clip.
slo.safetyNotes: Use sharp pencils and rulers safely. Learners remain seated while plotting. Keep the walking-out activity in a clear corridor or playground, with no running.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting what a picture of a parked matatu, a steady car and a returning cyclist would look like on a graph of displacement against time. They then observe the data tables for three Naivasha situations: a parked matatu at a stage 5 km from Naivasha town for 30 min; a steady car at 60 km/h with points (0,0), (30,30), (60,60) in (min, km); and cyclist Atieno going to the Lake Naivasha gate and back with points (0,0), (30,6), (40,6), (60,0). In the Explain phase they choose scales, plot and draw the graphs and describe each shape using only words such as flat, rising and falling. They add questions to the Driving Question Board and revise the class model by adding 'a graph can show how displacement changes with time'. No gradient or velocity is read from the graphs in this lesson; that is Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the overtaking clip (Car A, the blue Toyota Axio, steady at 72 km/h; Car B, the white Subaru, speeding up). On a blank axis sketch in their notebooks (t along the bottom, displacement up the side) they predict what the line would look like for three situations: (1) a matatu parked at a stage 5 km from Naivasha town for 30 min; (2) a car moving steadily at 60 km/h from Naivasha; (3) cyclist Atieno cycling from home to the Lake Naivasha gate and back home. They compare predictions with a partner and note one reason for each choice.
framework.teacherMoves: Draw three empty axes on the board. Say: 'Kiprono films the road and we want a picture of each movement. Sketch a line for each situation. There is no wrong answer yet, I want your best thinking.' Read each situation slowly. After the sketching, give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners with different sketches for the cyclist. Ask: 'What made you draw it going down at the end?' Record two or three sketches on the board without judging them. Say: 'We will test these with data.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (initial ideas elicitation): committing to a sketch before seeing data surfaces misconceptions (for example, that a parked vehicle gives a line going up, or that a graph is a picture of the road). Learners later compare the sketch with their drawn graph, which builds understanding through conflict and confirmation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) whether learners label t on the x-axis and displacement on the y-axis; (b) whether the parked matatu is drawn flat or sloping; (c) whether the cyclist's return is drawn falling. Tally on a class list how many sketch the parked matatu as a rising line, to target in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 with a data card for each situation. Parked matatu: displacement stays 5 km from Naivasha town for 30 min, with points (0,5), (15,5), (30,5) in (min, km). Steady car at 60 km/h: (0,0), (30,30), (60,60). Cyclist Atieno: (0,0), (30,6), (40,6), (60,0). Each group also acts out the cyclist's trip: one learner walks slowly away along a corridor for 'half the time', stands still for a short time, then walks back to the start while a timekeeper calls the phases and a recorder notes the position at each call. Learners notice that the position goes up, stays the same, then goes back to zero.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out the data cards and graph paper. Say: 'Look at the numbers first. Where does the cyclist's displacement go up, where does it stay the same, and where does it come back to zero?' Circulate and ask: 'Atieno ends at displacement 0. Where is she?' (back at home). Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to report what they notice in the table of the walking activity. Say: 'Positive means away from home; the return trip brings the displacement back to zero.' Remind learners that displacement has direction, as met in Lesson 2.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Embodied modelling with data tables: acting out the cyclist's trip connects the abstract numbers to a real movement, helping learners see why the displacement values rise, stay and fall before they plot them.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for statements such as 'the displacement does not change from 30 to 40 minutes' and 'it returns to 0 at 60 minutes'. Check that each group correctly identifies the three phases of Atieno's journey in the table. Note groups that confuse distance travelled with displacement.

framework.learnerExperience: Step 1 (scales): Learners decide how to fit the data on graph paper. For the cyclist: x-axis 0 to 60 min, with 1 cm = 10 min; y-axis 0 to 6 km, with 1 cm = 1 km. For the steady car: y-axis 0 to 60 km, with 1 cm = 10 km. For the parked matatu: y-axis from 0 to 6 km, 1 cm = 1 km. Step 2 (plot and draw): They label both axes with quantity and unit, plot each point with a small cross, and join points with a ruler. Step 3 (describe): They write one sentence per graph: the parked matatu gives a horizontal line at 5 km; the steady car gives a straight line rising from (0,0) to (60,60); the returning cyclist rises from (0,0) to (30,6), is flat to (40,6), then falls to (60,0). Step 4 (link): In pairs they discuss: 'The cyclist's line ends on the x-axis. What does that tell us about where Atieno is?' and 'How could Car A's steady motion in the overtaking clip look on a displacement-time graph?' (a straight rising line; shape only).
framework.teacherMoves: Model one scale choice on the board: 'The biggest time is 60 min and the page is 20 squares wide, so 1 cm for 10 min fits.' Ask: 'Why would 1 cm for 1 min not fit?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Walk around with a checklist: axes labelled with units, scale even, points plotted exactly, ruler used. Cold-call 3 learners to describe a graph using only the words 'flat', 'rising' and 'falling'. Say: 'Today we describe the shape only. In the next lesson we will find out what the steepness tells us.' Do not introduce gradient calculations. Ask: 'Which situation gives a line that comes back down? What does that tell us about the direction of the cyclist's movement?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Scaffolded procedure with talk moves (revoicing and peer checking): learners follow the sequence choose scale, plot, join, describe, then compare drawn graphs with their Predict sketches. Revoicing ('So you are saying the line is flat because the matatu is not moving away') links vocabulary to meaning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: scales are even and fit the page; axes have labels with units; all four cyclist points are correctly placed at (0,0), (30,6), (40,6), (60,0); the parked matatu line is horizontal; the steady car line passes through (30,30) and (60,60); descriptions use 'flat', 'rising' and 'falling' correctly. Collect one graph per learner as an exit check.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board. They place the new graphs beside the overtaking clip and add or answer questions, for example: 'What would Car B's graph look like when it speeds up?', 'How can we tell from a graph how fast the cyclist went?', 'Can we use graphs to know when two vehicles meet?' They mark questions about graph shape as partly answered, and move questions about steepness and meeting points to a 'coming next' column.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which of our questions can the graphs help us answer today?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds and cold-call 3 learners to read or add a question. Ask: 'Which questions need us to read the graph, not just draw it?' Place sticky notes under the labels 'answered in part' and 'next lesson'. Say: 'Next lesson we will read the cyclist's graph to find velocity.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board tracking: showing what has been learned and what remains builds ownership and keeps the phenomenon (how one car overtakes another) connected to each skill. Sorting questions by status makes progress visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that new questions refer to the graph skills (shape, steepness, meeting, speeding up) and to the overtaking. Note learners whose questions show they see a graph as a tool for describing and predicting motion.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update their class model for the driving question. In their notebooks they add a section titled 'Graphs of motion' with the three graphs drawn small, each labelled with its situation and shape: parked matatu (flat line), steady car (straight rising line), returning cyclist (rises, flat, falls to zero). Under them they write: 'A displacement-time graph shows how displacement changes as time passes.' They add a sketch showing where Car A, which moves steadily, could be placed on such a graph, and a note: 'Car B's motion changes; we still need a way to show this.' Then they complete the summary table prompts.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add what you can now show that you could not show before. Use the words flat, rising and falling.' Walk round and ask: 'Which shape would Car A have?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to share their model additions. Ask: 'What is still missing from our model of the overtaking?' Expect: speeds, steepness, Car B's change, relative motion. Close with: 'Next lesson we interpret these graphs.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding the new graph tool to the model, and naming what is still missing, helps learners see how each lesson contributes to the final answer to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each notebook for: three correctly labelled graph sketches; accurate shape descriptions; a clear statement of what a displacement-time graph shows; an identification of at least one gap in the model. Use a 3-point rubric (complete, partly complete, needs support).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners chose workable scales without help, and which needed the 'biggest value fits the page' prompt? Did the walking activity help learners see why the cyclist's line returns to zero? Which learners treated the graph as a picture of the road? Were you able to keep the focus on drawing and describing shape, without drifting into gradient calculations that belong to Lesson 5? What would you change in the data cards to support learners who plot slowly?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed data for a parked matatu 5 km from Naivasha town, a steady car at 60 km/h with points (0,0), (30,30), (60,60), and cyclist Atieno with points (0,0), (30,6), (40,6), (60,0) in (min, km). We saw that the displacement stays the same, rises steadily, or returns to zero.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned to choose scales, label axes with units, plot points and join them with a ruler to draw displacement-time graphs. A parked vehicle gives a horizontal line, a steady car gives a straight rising line, and a returning cyclist gives a line that rises, goes flat and then falls to zero.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can draw a graph of displacement against time for a stationary, steady or returning movement and describe its shape. This helps us describe the steady motion of Car A in the overtaking, and shows we need more tools, such as reading steepness and velocity-time graphs, to describe Car B speeding up.
