LESSONS.title: Interpreting Displacement-Time Graphs: Gradient, Rest and Meeting Points
LESSONS.aresKeywords: displacement-time graph, gradient, velocity, direction, negative gradient, rest, flat line, intersection, meeting point, Naivasha, Nakuru, cyclist Atieno, matatu

slo.purpose: Learners read information from displacement-time graphs: velocity as the gradient (sign shows direction), rest as a flat line, and the meeting point of two bodies as the intersection of their graphs. They use this to move closer to describing and predicting the overtake on the Naivasha highway.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) state that the gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity; (2) explain that a positive gradient means moving towards Nakuru (or away from home) and a negative gradient means moving the other way; (3) identify a flat line as rest (velocity 0); (4) find the meeting point of two bodies as the intersection of their graphs.
slo.skills: Calculating gradient as change in displacement divided by change in time (building on Lesson 3's velocity calculation); reading values from a graph drawn in Lesson 4; analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP 4); using mathematics and computational thinking (SEP 5); constructing explanations from graph evidence (SEP 6); communicating and collaborating in pairs.
slo.attitudes: Appreciating that graphs are a powerful tool for describing and predicting real motion on Kenyan roads; accuracy and patience when reading scales; willingness to justify claims with evidence; respect for road safety.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? (Here: from the gradient of its displacement-time graph.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 4 learners drew displacement-time graphs, and in Lesson 3 they calculated velocity as displacement/time. Lesson 5 turns those graphs into evidence: learners read velocity, direction and rest from them and find where two vehicles meet. This answers the DQB questions 'how do we tell how fast and in which direction?' and prepares for velocity-time graphs in Lessons 6 and 7. A lorry coming towards a car is the same kind of situation as the Naivasha-Nakuru meeting problem, a two-graph meeting, which links to the oncoming lorry L in the phenomenon. Relative speed and safety margins are not calculated here; those come in Lessons 8 and 9.
slo.safetyNotes: This is a paper and graph lesson. Learners remain seated; use sharp pencils safely. If any outdoor walking demonstration of constant speed is used, keep it in a cleared area away from the road. Remind learners never to experiment with overtaking or racing on real roads, and always to cross roads at safe places.

LESSONS.overview: Learners start with the overtaking puzzle in mind: how do we describe and predict motion with numbers and graphs? They predict what different graph shapes mean for the returning cyclist Atieno (Naivasha to Lake Naivasha gate and back). In the Observe phase they work in pairs with the graph drawn in Lesson 4, points (0,0), (30,6), (40,6), (60,0) in (min,km), and calculate the gradient of each section: 12 km/h, 0 and -18 km/h. In the Explain phase they use two graphs on the same axes for a matatu leaving Naivasha at 60 km/h and a private car leaving Nakuru at 90 km/h, 60 km apart, and find that they meet after 24 minutes, 24 km from Naivasha. They add new questions to the Driving Question Board and update their model by recording that gradient gives velocity and sign gives direction, and that the oncoming lorry L would have a negative gradient on the same graph as the cars A and B moving towards Nakuru. No new numbers for the overtaking are introduced beyond what learners already know; the speeds of A (20 m/s) and the lorry (-20 m/s) are used only as examples of the sign of the gradient.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the overtaking clip near Naivasha and the DQB question 'how can we tell how fast and in which direction a vehicle is moving?' The teacher displays the graph for cyclist Atieno drawn in Lesson 4 with points (0,0), (30,6), (40,6), (60,0) in (min,km), with the sections not yet labelled. Individually, learners write a prediction in their notebooks for three questions: (a) Which part shows Atieno riding fastest? (b) What is happening where the line is flat? (c) What does the last part, where the line goes down, mean? They also predict: 'If a matatu leaves Naivasha for Nakuru and a car leaves Nakuru for Naivasha at the same time, where on a graph would we see them meet?' Learners sketch this in 2 minutes and share with a partner. This connects to the oncoming lorry L, which also travels in the opposite direction to the cars.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the graph and say: 'You drew this graph last lesson. Do not calculate yet. Look at the three sections and write what you think each one tells us about Atieno's ride.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing. WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds after asking 'What does a flat line mean?' before taking any answer. Cold-call 3 learners with 'Achieng, what did you predict for the middle section? Kiprono, do you agree? Why?' Then ask: 'In the overtaking clip, the lorry L comes towards the cars from Nakuru. If we drew all of them on one graph, how might its line look different from the car's line?' Take 2 more predictions without evaluating. Record predictions on the board under the heading 'Our predictions' to revisit at the end. Say: 'Today we will test these predictions with calculations and graphs.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Prediction Recording): learners commit to ideas in writing before instruction. This surfaces the common idea that a steeper line means 'higher up' rather than 'faster' and that a falling line means 'slowing down' rather than 'coming back'. Because predictions are written down and revisited, learners see how evidence changes their ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe and record: how many learners write that a flat line means 'stopped' or 'not moving' (correct) versus 'moving at steady speed' (misconception)? How many predict that the downward section means 'slowing down' (common misconception) versus 'coming back'? Note whether learners can sketch two lines that cross and say that the crossing shows a meeting. Use a thumbs-up/thumbs-down check on 'a steeper line means faster' and tally the count on the board.

framework.learnerExperience: In pairs, learners use the graph of Atieno's ride, points (0,0), (30,6), (40,6), (60,0) in (min,km), and a worksheet. Task 1: For each of the three sections, read the change in displacement and the change in time from the graph and calculate the gradient. Section 1 (0-30 min): 6 km in 30 min = 0.2 km/min = 12 km/h. Section 2 (30-40 min): 0 km in 10 min = 0 km/h (the flat line, resting at 6 km). Section 3 (40-60 min): -6 km in 20 min = -0.3 km/min = -18 km/h. Learners convert km/min to km/h by multiplying by 60. They label each section with a velocity and a direction in words: 'away from home at 12 km/h', 'at rest', 'back towards home at 18 km/h'. Task 2: Learners compare the steepness of sections 1 and 3 and say why section 3 is steeper and slopes down. They recall that Atieno's final displacement is 0 and her total distance is 12 km. Task 3: Learners compare with a steady car at 60 km/h, points (0,0), (30,30), (60,60) in (min,km), and check that the gradient is 30 km / 30 min = 1 km/min = 60 km/h. They link the sign of velocity to the oncoming lorry L, whose velocity is -20 m/s because it travels towards Naivasha while the positive direction is towards Nakuru.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute worksheets and rulers. Say: 'Choose two points on the straight section, find how far up the line goes and how far across, then divide up by across. Show units.' Circulate and ask each pair: 'What does your answer tell us about how fast Atieno is going? In which direction?' WAIT TIME: after asking 'Why is the gradient of the last section negative?' wait 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 4 pairs: one for each section's gradient and one for the steady car. Ask: 'Which is faster, 12 km/h or -18 km/h? Careful: what does the minus sign tell you and what does the number tell you?' Draw out that the number is the speed and the sign is the direction. Point to the lorry: 'The lorry L has velocity -20 m/s. What would its line on a displacement-time graph do?' Take 2 responses. Address the misconception that a flat line means constant speed by asking: 'If the line is flat, has the displacement changed? So what is the velocity?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Analysis and Pattern Finding with Structured Calculation: learners compute the same quantity (gradient) from three differently-shaped sections and notice the pattern: steeper means faster, upward means positive, downward means negative, flat means zero. Repeating the same calculation on different sections builds a general rule that links the graph to the velocity formula from Lesson 3.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check worksheets for: gradients 12 km/h, 0 and -18 km/h with units; correct conversion from km/min to km/h; correct labelling of direction in words. Look for learners who compute the gradient as 'time divided by displacement' and prompt them to check the units. Use a quick exit signal: learners hold up fingers 1, 2 or 3 for the section with the greatest speed (answer: 3). Record how many pairs correctly explain that the minus sign shows direction, not 'smaller speed'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners explain how graphs help solve the Naivasha-Nakuru meeting problem, which is similar to the oncoming lorry L approaching the cars. Setting: Naivasha and Nakuru are 60 km apart. A matatu leaves Naivasha for Nakuru at 60 km/h and a private car leaves Nakuru for Naivasha at 90 km/h at the same moment. Taking displacement from Naivasha, learners work out two lines: the matatu (0,0) to (60 min, 60 km), and the car starting at 60 km at 0 min with velocity -90 km/h, reaching (40 min, 0 km) after 40 min. Using a scale such as 1 cm = 5 min and 1 cm = 5 km, they draw both lines on one pair of axes and find the point where the lines cross: at 24 min and 24 km from Naivasha. They check with calculation: matatu 60 x 0.4 = 24 km; car 90 x 0.4 = 36 km; 24 + 36 = 60 km. They write a short explanation: 'The two lines cross at 24 min and 24 km because at that moment both vehicles are at the same place at the same time.' Learners then return to the Atieno graph and revise their predictions. Finally they explain how a graph could describe the overtake: car A would be a straight line with gradient 20 m/s, car B would curve upward at first because its velocity increases, and lorry L would slope downwards with gradient -20 m/s. They do not calculate relative speed yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Two vehicles are at the same place at the same time. What would that look like on a graph?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners for ideas. Guide the drawing step by step: 'Where does the matatu start? Where does the car start? Which line goes up and which goes down? Why?' Circulate and check each pair's scales. When pairs find the intersection, ask: 'How can we check this answer without the graph?' Cold-call 2 pairs to show the check 60 x 0.4 = 24 and 90 x 0.4 = 36. Ask: 'In the overtaking clip, the lorry L is coming towards the cars. Would its line go up or down on a graph where up is towards Nakuru? Why?' Cold-call 2 learners. Ask: 'Car A has a steady velocity of 20 m/s. What would its line look like?' Accept 'a straight upward line'. Ask: 'Car B speeds up at first. Predict how the shape of its line would differ.' Do not give the answer: say 'We will test that idea in later lessons when we study velocity and acceleration.' Return to the prediction board and ask learners to circle correct predictions and correct the others using evidence from the graph.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Graph Intersection: learners make a claim (the vehicles meet at 24 min and 24 km), support it with evidence from the graph and calculation, and give reasoning (same place, same time). Using two representations, the graph and the arithmetic check, builds understanding that the intersection means the same displacement at the same time. Revisiting the lorry L from the phenomenon transfers the idea to the overtaking puzzle.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: both lines correctly drawn with the car line sloping downwards; intersection read as 24 min and 24 km; calculation check 24 + 36 = 60; correct statement that the negative gradient means moving towards Naivasha. Listen for the explanation that the intersection shows 'same place, same time'. Note whether learners confuse the intersection with equal speed (misconception) and probe: 'Are the two speeds equal? What is equal at the meeting point?' Use a 3-minute mini-quiz with one problem: 'A graph line goes from (0,0) to (10 min, 5 km) then is flat to 20 min. State the velocity in each section.' Expected: 0.5 km/min = 30 km/h, then 0.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board. In groups of four, they write new questions on sticky notes and sort them into categories: 'what we now know', 'what we still need to find out'. Examples of what they now know: 'Gradient of a displacement-time graph gives velocity'; 'a negative gradient means moving in the opposite direction, like the oncoming lorry L'; 'a flat line means at rest'; 'the intersection of two graphs shows where and when two vehicles meet'. Examples of new questions: 'How do we show that Car B speeds up on a graph?', 'What does a graph of velocity against time look like?', 'How can we find the distance from a velocity graph?', 'Why does Car A look slow from Car B when both speedometers show high speeds?', 'How long does the overtaking take?'. Learners place the notes under the two KICD questions: 'How do you determine the velocity of a moving body?' (partly answered today: from the gradient) and 'How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body?' (not yet answered).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our Driving Question Board. Which questions can we now answer after today? Move those notes to the answered column and give the evidence.' Cold-call 3 groups to move a note and justify it. WAIT TIME: after asking 'What new question has today's work raised?' wait 10-15 seconds before taking responses. Ask: 'Our graph of the meeting matatu and car shows a straight line for each, because each had a steady velocity. What about Car B, which speeds up? What question does that raise?' Guide learners to the idea that a different kind of graph is needed, without teaching it. Ensure at least 2 new questions point towards velocity-time graphs and 1 towards relative speed. Take a photograph or copy the board for later use.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question Sorting and Tracking Progress on the DQB: learners categorise questions as answered, partly answered or open, using evidence from the lesson. This shows how each lesson adds one piece to the overall puzzle and motivates the next lesson by making gaps in understanding visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check whether each group moves at least one question with correct evidence, e.g. 'velocity is the gradient' with the Atieno figures 12, 0 and -18 km/h. Look for new questions that go beyond recall, such as asking about acceleration or relative speed. Note groups whose questions show the misconception that the displacement-time graph of an accelerating car is straight; these learners need the follow-up in Lessons 6 and 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add to their cumulative model of the overtake. On a page headed 'Our model of the overtaking on the Naivasha highway', they add a new section called 'Reading displacement-time graphs'. They record: (1) Velocity = gradient = change in displacement / change in time; (2) positive gradient = towards Nakuru (positive direction); negative gradient = towards Naivasha, like the oncoming lorry L with velocity -20 m/s; (3) flat line = at rest, velocity 0 (like the parked matatu); (4) the meeting point of two bodies is where their lines cross: same time, same place. They draw a small sketch with three lines on one pair of axes: Car A (steady upward line), the lorry L (steady downward line) and a question mark for Car B, noting 'B speeds up, so its line is not straight; we need to find out more.' They then complete a short reflection: 'Today I learned that ... I am still wondering ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your model page. Add today's evidence under the new heading and make sure that you use the numbers from Atieno's ride and the matatu and car meeting.' Circulate and ask 3 learners: 'How does today's idea help us explain the overtake? What is still missing?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds before each answer. Cold-call 3 learners to read their sketch. Ask: 'Why have you put a question mark for Car B?' Accept: 'its velocity changes so its graph would not have a constant gradient'. Close with: 'Next time we will draw a different kind of graph, velocity against time, to show how Car B speeds up.' Collect model pages as a record of progress. Revisit the predictions on the board and mark them right or wrong with learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: learners add to a growing model, linking each new idea to the anchoring phenomenon. Explicitly marking what the model cannot yet explain (Car B's speeding up) builds the habit of identifying the limits of a model and motivates the next investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check model pages for: all four statements recorded with correct figures (12, 0, -18 km/h; 24 min and 24 km); a correct sketch showing lines of opposite gradients; a clear statement of what is still unknown. Use the reflection sentence as an exit ticket and sort into: ready for velocity-time graphs, needs practice on reading gradient with units, needs support on negative gradient. Plan short revision on any group not reaching the expected explanation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners calculate the gradients 12 km/h, 0 and -18 km/h correctly with units? Which misconceptions were most common (flat line means constant speed; downward line means slowing down; intersection means equal speeds)? Did learners link the negative gradient to the oncoming lorry L? Were scales on the meeting graph chosen sensibly, and who needed support with plotting? Which DQB questions were raised that should be addressed in Lessons 6 to 9? How will you adjust the next lesson to build on learners' readiness to move from displacement-time to velocity-time graphs?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the graph of Atieno's ride has three sections with gradients 12 km/h, 0 and -18 km/h, and that the lines for the matatu leaving Naivasha at 60 km/h and the car leaving Nakuru at 90 km/h cross at 24 min and 24 km from Naivasha.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity, that its sign shows direction (negative means the opposite way, like the oncoming lorry L), that a flat line means rest, and that the intersection of two graphs shows where and when two bodies meet.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the vehicles meet when their graphs cross because they are at the same displacement at the same time. This helps us describe the motion of Car A, Car B and the oncoming lorry L, but we still need velocity-time graphs and acceleration to explain how Car B speeds up when overtaking.

LESSONS.title: Drawing Velocity-Time Graphs: Speeding Up, Steady Speed and Slowing Down
LESSONS.aresKeywords: velocity-time graph, rising line, horizontal line, falling line, acceleration, deceleration, scale, plotting

slo.purpose: Learners plot velocity-time graphs from data tables and recognise the shapes for speeding up (rising line), steady speed (horizontal line) and slowing down (falling line), so that they can describe the motion of Car B, Car A and a braking matatu on the Nairobi-Nakuru highway.
slo.knowledge: Learners will: (1) state that a velocity-time graph has t (s) on the x-axis and v (m/s) on the y-axis; (2) match a rising line to speeding up (positive acceleration), a horizontal line to steady speed (zero acceleration) and a falling line to slowing down (deceleration, negative acceleration); (3) link the 2 m/s^2 and -2 m/s^2 already calculated in Lesson 3 to the shapes they draw.
slo.skills: Learners will: choose a scale (1 cm = 1 s on the x-axis, a suitable scale on the y-axis); plot points from a table; join them with a ruler or a straight edge; label axes with units; describe the shape of each section of a graph in words (SEP 4: Analysing and Interpreting Data; SEP 2: Developing and Using Models).
slo.attitudes: Learners will show accuracy and neatness when plotting, persevere when a point looks wrong, and cooperate respectfully when checking a partner's graph.
slo.keyInquiry: How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body? (This lesson shows how velocity values from a table become a picture whose shape tells us whether the body is speeding up, moving steadily or slowing down. Gradient and area are interpreted in Lesson 7.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 4 gave learners the skill of plotting displacement-time graphs and Lesson 3 gave the acceleration values (B: 2 m/s^2; braking matatu: -2 m/s^2). Lesson 6 turns the velocity data of Car B, Car A and the braking matatu into velocity-time graphs. These graphs are the tool learners will interpret in Lesson 7 (gradient and area) and use in Lesson 8 (relative speed) to explain why A looks slow from B.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners work at desks with rulers and sharp pencils: handle pencils and compasses carefully and keep them away from faces. Use the videos only for seated viewing. When discussing overtaking, remind learners that real overtaking on Kenyan roads is dangerous and that they must never try to copy it, and must always cross roads at safe points.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the Naivasha overtaking clip. Achieng watches the speedometers from the back seat of Car B, so learners predict what her speedometer readings would look like as a picture. They then plot three velocity-time graphs from tables: Car B (t = 0 to 7.5 s, v from 20 to 30 m/s), Car A (constant 20 m/s) and the braking matatu (t = 0 to 10 s, v from 20 to 0 m/s). They compare the three shapes, name them as speeding up, steady speed and slowing down, and connect each shape to the acceleration already calculated in Lesson 3. Learners update the DQB and add the graphs to their class model of the overtake.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the clip of Wanjiru's white Subaru (Car B) overtaking Mr Kamau's blue Toyota Axio (Car A) near Naivasha. Achieng, in the back seat of Car B, writes down the speedometer readings: 72 km/h at the start, then higher. Individually, learners sketch on a blank axis (t on x, v on y) what they think a picture of Car A's speed and Car B's speed against time would look like, using two colours. They do not yet have the table. They then pair up and compare sketches.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the question: 'If Achieng wrote her speedometer reading every second, what would the picture look like for Car A and for Car B?' Say: 'Draw your best idea. There is no wrong prediction today; we will test it.' Circulate and ask 3 pairs: 'What does your line for Car A do, and why?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question before accepting an answer. Cold-call 4 learners to describe their sketch for Car B and 2 for Car A. Record two or three different predictions on the board without judging them, e.g. 'B jumps straight up', 'B rises gradually', 'A is flat'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE): committing to a prediction before seeing the data creates a reason to examine the evidence, and the gap between prediction and graph exposes ideas such as 'speed changes instantly'.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (a) put t on the x-axis and v on the y-axis, (b) draw Car A as flat or constant, (c) show Car B higher than or rising from Car A. Note on a checklist the number of learners who draw B as a sudden jump versus a gradual rise to use in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 with graph paper, rulers and the three data tables. Table 1, Car B: t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7.5 s with v = 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 30, 30, 30 m/s. Table 2, Car A: v = 20 m/s at every time from 0 to 7.5 s. Table 3, braking matatu: t = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 s with v = 20, 16, 12, 8, 4, 0 m/s. Using the scale 1 cm = 1 s on the x-axis and, for example, 1 cm = 2 m/s on the y-axis, each learner plots Graph 1 (Cars A and B on the same axes, in two colours), then Graph 2 (the braking matatu). They label axes with units (t (s), v (m/s)), join points with a ruler, and write a title for each graph. Learners give each section of each line a word description, e.g. 'rises steadily from 20 to 30 m/s between 0 and 5 s'.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first two points of Car B on the board or projector, thinking aloud: 'The scale is 1 cm for 1 s across. Which scale on the vertical axis lets 0 to 30 m/s fit on the page?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 2 groups for their scale choice. Remind learners of the plotting skills from Lesson 4 by asking: 'What must every axis have?' (label and units). Circulate and check points; when you see an error ask: 'Does this point agree with the table? Check t first, then v.' Ask each group: 'Why is Car A's line the same height every second?' Cold-call 3 learners to explain. Ask a group that finishes early: 'Where does Car B's line stop rising, and what does Achieng's speedometer show after that?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-to-representation modelling (SEP 4 and SEP 2): turning numbers in a table into a picture lets learners see patterns (rising, flat, falling) that are hard to spot in columns, and plotting on the same axes lets them compare A and B directly.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each graph for: axes labelled with units; correct scale (1 cm = 1 s); all points plotted within half a small square; straight line drawn with a ruler; Car A horizontal at 20 m/s; Car B rising from 20 m/s at t = 0 to 30 m/s at t = 5 s then horizontal to 7.5 s; matatu falling from 20 m/s at t = 0 to 0 m/s at t = 10 s. Record how many groups need help with scale and with joining points.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups compare their three lines and complete a sentence frame for each: 'The line is ______, so the vehicle is ______.' They classify: rising line = speeding up; horizontal line = steady speed; falling line = slowing down. They link each shape to the acceleration from Lesson 3: Car B a = (30 - 20)/5 = 2 m/s^2 (positive, speeding up), Car A a = 0 (steady), matatu a = (0 - 20)/10 = -2 m/s^2 (deceleration 2 m/s^2). They revisit their Predict sketches and explain what they got right and what changed, for example that Car B reaches 30 m/s gradually over 5 s rather than at once. They also answer: 'On the graph, in which part of the overtake is Car B speeding up and in which part is it steady?' (speeding up for 0-5 s, steady from 5 s to 7.5 s). Finally, they write one sentence about what the graph does NOT yet tell them (how far each car has travelled, covered in Lesson 7).
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up two learner graphs and ask: 'What is the same and what is different about the lines for Car B and the braking matatu?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners. Press for evidence: 'Point to the part of the graph that shows that.' Ask: 'Car B's graph is rising and the matatu's graph is falling. How do the signs of the accelerations 2 and -2 match this?' Cold-call 3 learners. Use the everyday words 'speed up' and 'slow down' first and then insist on 'acceleration' and 'deceleration' for formal answers. Correct the common misconception that a horizontal line means the car is stopped: ask 'Car A is on a horizontal line at 20 m/s; is it parked?' and let learners discuss in pairs for 1 minute. Say: 'Before we do gradient and area in the next lesson, just describe the shape.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with sentence frames: learners state a claim ('Car B is speeding up from 0 to 5 s'), cite evidence from the graph (rising line from 20 to 30 m/s), and reason using the acceleration value from Lesson 3. This builds a link between representation and meaning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for learners who (a) say a horizontal line at 20 m/s means steady speed, not stopped; (b) say the falling line means deceleration and write a = -2 m/s^2; (c) quote numbers from the graph as evidence. Use an exit-ticket question: 'Sketch the velocity-time shape for a matatu that speeds up, then travels steadily, then slows down.' Look for rising, horizontal, falling in the right order.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class Driving Question Board from Lesson 1 and from the questions about 'how far' and 'how fast'. In groups they sort the questions into: answered by this lesson (e.g. 'Does Car B speed up all the time?'), partly answered (e.g. 'How far do the cars travel?'), and not yet answered (e.g. 'Why does A look slow from B?', 'Was the overtake safe?'). They write one new question on a sticky note arising from the graphs, such as 'What do the gradient and the area under Car B's line tell us?' and place it on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which questions can we now answer using our graphs?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to move one sticky note each and explain why. Ask: 'What new question do these graphs make you ask?' Collect at least 4 new questions. Point out that the question 'How far?' needs something more from the graph, which the class will explore in Lesson 7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board routine: sorting questions by what has been answered keeps the investigation purposeful and shows learners how each piece of evidence moves them towards answering the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that new questions are linked to the graphs and to the phenomenon, for example about distance or relative speed, rather than random. Note how many learners can explain why a question is only partly answered.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add a new panel to the class model of the overtake: a velocity-time graph poster with Car A (horizontal line at 20 m/s) and Car B (rising line from 20 to 30 m/s over 0-5 s, then horizontal to 7.5 s) on the same axes, with the key moments marked: t = 0 B starts to accelerate; t = 5 s B reaches 30 m/s; t = 7.5 s overtaking complete. Beside the graph they write labels such as 'speeding up, a = 2 m/s^2' and 'steady speed, a = 0'. They add a small side panel for the braking matatu labelled 'slowing down, deceleration 2 m/s^2'. Finally, each learner completes the summary table and writes one sentence on how the model now explains the speed changes of the overtaking car B.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must show what the speedometers did. Where on your graph does Wanjiru reach 108 km/h?' Cold-call 2 learners (answer: 30 m/s, at t = 5 s; 30 x 3.6 = 108 km/h). Ask: 'How does your model explain that both cars look fast on the speedometer?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'What can your model not yet tell us?' (distance travelled, relative speed, safety). Ask groups to peer review another group's poster using a 3-point checklist: axes with units, correct shapes, labels.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding the velocity-time graph to the class model connects the new representation to earlier ideas (velocity, acceleration) and to the phenomenon, and shows which parts of the explanation are still missing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each model for: correct graph of Car A and Car B on the same axes; labelled sections; units; links to the 2 m/s^2 acceleration. Ask 3 learners to explain their model in one minute and look for correct use of 'speeding up', 'steady speed', 'slowing down', 'acceleration' and 'deceleration'.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners chose a suitable scale on their own and which needed help? Did any learners treat a horizontal line as 'not moving', and how did the discussion of Car A's steady 20 m/s address this? Were the predicted sketches in the Predict Phase different from the final graphs (for example, did anyone draw B jumping instantly to 30 m/s)? How well did learners connect the shape of each line to the accelerations 2 m/s^2, 0 and -2 m/s^2 from Lesson 3? What preparation (pre-printed grids, rulers, pencils) would help in the next lesson, where learners interpret gradient and area?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe? Example: Car A's velocity-time graph is a horizontal line at 20 m/s. Car B's graph rises in a straight line from 20 m/s at t = 0 to 30 m/s at t = 5 s and then is horizontal until t = 7.5 s. The braking matatu's graph falls in a straight line from 20 m/s at t = 0 to 0 m/s at t = 10 s.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? Example: A rising line shows speeding up (positive acceleration, e.g. 2 m/s^2), a horizontal line shows steady speed (zero acceleration), and a falling line shows slowing down (deceleration, e.g. a = -2 m/s^2). A velocity-time graph has t (s) on the x-axis and v (m/s) on the y-axis.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How does this help us explain the overtake? Example: The graphs show that Wanjiru in Car B speeds up gradually from 72 km/h to 108 km/h in 5 s and then holds that speed, while Mr Kamau in Car A stays at 72 km/h. Next we need to find how far each car travels and how their speeds compare.

LESSONS.title: Interpreting Velocity-Time Graphs: Gradient for Acceleration, Area for Distance
LESSONS.aresKeywords: velocity-time graph, gradient, acceleration, deceleration, area under graph, trapezium, rectangle, triangle, distance travelled, stopping distance

slo.purpose: Learners interpret velocity-time graphs of the overtaking cars and a braking matatu to find acceleration or deceleration from the gradient and distance travelled from the area under the graph, then check the answers against the split-time table.
slo.knowledge: Gradient of a velocity-time graph = acceleration, a = (v - u)/t, in m/s^2. A negative gradient means deceleration. The area under a velocity-time graph = distance travelled (displacement when velocity does not change sign). Areas are found using a trapezium, rectangle and triangle.
slo.skills: Calculating gradients from graph points; splitting the area under a graph into a trapezium, rectangle and triangle; calculating areas with units; checking graph results against a data table; communicating reasoning (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking).
slo.attitudes: Accuracy, perseverance, curiosity about road safety, and respect for others' reasoning during discussion.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? 2. How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 6 gave learners velocity-time graphs drawn from tables for Car B, Car A and the braking matatu. Lesson 5 gave gradient as a rate. Lesson 7 turns those graphs into numbers: B's acceleration of 2 m/s^2 and the distances 200 m (B) and 150 m (A). These distances are needed in Lesson 8 (relative speed and the 50 m gained) and Lesson 9 (the safety margin).
slo.safetyNotes: Learners work seated at desks with rulers, pencils and graph paper. Remind them to keep pencils and rulers on the desk. In the discussion on overtaking, stress that the numbers describe a model, and that real drivers should never overtake without a clear view of the road.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the Naivasha highway overtaking clip and their Lesson 6 velocity-time graphs for Car B (20 to 30 m/s in 5 s, then steady to 7.5 s) and Car A (steady 20 m/s). They predict what the slope and the shaded region under the line might mean. They find the gradient of B's sloping section (2 m/s^2) and the gradient of the braking matatu's line (-2 m/s^2). They split the area under B's graph into a trapezium (125 m) and a rectangle (75 m), giving 200 m, and the area under A's graph (150 m). They then check these against the split-time table. They add the new evidence to the Driving Question Board (DQB) and revise their model of the overtake.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the Lesson 6 velocity-time graph of Car B and Car A on the same axes (1 cm = 1 s on the x-axis). Individually they write for 2 minutes: (a) what does the slope of B's line from 0 to 5 s tell us about the white Subaru driven by Wanjiru? (b) Could the shaded space between the line and the time axis tell us how far B travelled? Pairs share predictions and write a number guess for B's distance in 7.5 s and A's distance in 7.5 s, using what they know from the clip.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the graph on the board or on a large chart. Say: "Remember the overtaking clip near Naivasha. Wanjiru in Car B sped up while Mr Kamau in Car A kept steady. Look at the two lines. What might the slope be telling us? What might the space under each line be telling us? Write your idea before you speak." Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking any answer. Cold-call 4 learners (2 for slope, 2 for area) and record predictions on a chart headed 'Our predictions'. Do not confirm or correct. Say: "Today we test these ideas with evidence."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage): making predictions visible lets learners compare their ideas with evidence later, helping them see that graphs carry information, not just shapes. It links directly to the phenomenon of how long and how far the overtake takes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: learners who connect the steeper line to B speeding up; learners who suggest the area relates to distance (even loosely, e.g. 'the space is how far'); learners who guess B's distance is more than A's. Note on a checklist which learners predicted distance and which were unsure, to guide questioning later.

framework.learnerExperience: Part 1, gradient: in pairs, learners use their own Lesson 6 graph of Car B. They mark two points on the sloping section, (0, 20) and (5, 30), draw a right-angled triangle and calculate gradient = change in v / change in t = (30 - 20)/5 = 2 m/s^2. They calculate the gradient of the flat sections: Car A from 0 to 7.5 s and Car B from 5 to 7.5 s, getting 0. They then take the braking matatu graph (points (0, 20), (2, 16), (4, 12), (6, 8), (8, 4), (10, 0)) and calculate gradient = (0 - 20)/10 = -2 m/s^2, writing 'deceleration 2 m/s^2'. Part 2, area: learners shade the region under B's line and split it into a trapezium from 0 to 5 s with area 1/2 x (20 + 30) x 5 = 125 m and a rectangle from 5 to 7.5 s with area 30 x 2.5 = 75 m, total 200 m. They calculate A's rectangle: 20 x 7.5 = 150 m. They calculate the matatu's triangle: 1/2 x 20 x 10 = 100 m stopping distance. Part 3, check: learners compare with the split-time table (B distance 200 m and A distance 150 m at 7.5 s; B at 5 s = 125 m, matching the trapezium). They also find B minus A = 50 m.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Say: "Show me the two points you chose. Which one is (t, v)? What are the units of your answer?" Prompt: "Why is the gradient of Car A's line zero? What does that say about its acceleration?" For the matatu: "Your answer is negative. What does the negative sign tell us about the matatu?" Insist on 'deceleration 2 m/s^2 means a = -2 m/s^2'. For area: "Which shape fits 0 to 5 s? Which fits 5 to 7.5 s? Name them before you calculate." Stop the class after the trapezium and ask for WAIT TIME of 10 seconds: "How can we check 125 m without using the graph?" Direct learners to the split-time table. Cold-call 3 pairs to report their totals (B 200 m, A 150 m, matatu 100 m). Support slower learners with a pre-drawn shaded graph; extend faster learners by asking them to find the area under A's line from 0 to 5 s (100 m) and compare with the table.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Analysis with Triangulation: learners find the same quantity two ways (graph area and the split-time table), which builds confidence that the area under a velocity-time graph is distance, and that the gradient is acceleration. This answers the KICD inquiry question on how to determine acceleration.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: correct gradient 2 m/s^2 with units; correct sign -2 m/s^2 for the matatu; correct split of B's area into a trapezium and a rectangle; correct totals 125 + 75 = 200 m, 150 m, 100 m; learners naming the match with the table without being told. Common errors to note: dividing time by velocity change, forgetting the 1/2 in the trapezium or triangle formula, using 7.5 instead of 2.5 for the rectangle width, and reporting a negative distance.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 learners prepare a short explanation titled 'What the graph tells us about the overtake': (1) Why does B's line slope up for 5 s and then go flat? (2) Why is B's distance (200 m) bigger than A's (150 m), and what does the 50 m difference represent in the real road (20 m starting gap + 5 m + 5 m car lengths + 20 m finishing gap)? (3) How do we know from the matatu graph that it slows down at a steady rate? Each group writes one sentence for gradient and one for area using the frame 'The gradient of the line is ... which means ...' and 'The area under the line is ... which means ...'. Learners also answer: what would the line for an oncoming lorry L look like at -20 m/s, and why would its area need care (direction)?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Wanjiru's friend Achieng watched the speedometer from the back seat of Car B. Use your graph to explain what she saw from 0 to 5 s and from 5 to 7.5 s." Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups. Probe with: "How do you know?", "What evidence in the table agrees?" and "What does 2 m/s^2 mean in words?" (speed increases by 2 m/s every second: 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30). Address the misconception that a bigger speed means larger acceleration: ask "Car A is at 20 m/s and B is at 30 m/s later. Which has the greater acceleration at 6 s?" (both zero). Link the 50 m to the milestone that B is level with A's front at 5 s (gained 25 m) and complete at 7.5 s (gained 50 m). Say: "Next lesson we will explain why A looks slow from B using relative speed."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): each group states a claim (e.g. B travels 200 m while A travels 150 m), supports it with evidence (areas and the split-time table) and gives reasoning (area under a v-t graph equals distance). This builds a scientific habit of justifying numbers and ties the mathematics back to the overtaking phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: groups explain that a sloping line means changing speed and a flat line means steady speed; groups connect 2 m/s^2 to 'gains 2 m/s each second'; groups state area = distance with units; groups justify the 50 m difference with the gap and car lengths. Use a 3-level checklist: states the number only; states the number with meaning; states the number, meaning and evidence from the table.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the DQB from Lesson 1. Using sticky notes they add (a) answers to earlier questions about 'how far' and 'how fast', e.g. 'B travels 200 m and A travels 150 m in 7.5 s (areas under graphs)', and 'B accelerates at 2 m/s^2 (gradient)'; (b) new questions, e.g. 'Why does A look slow from B if both speedometers read high?', 'Is there enough road before the lorry arrives?'. Each learner places at least one note and explains it to a neighbour.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at our board. Which questions can we now answer with graph evidence? Move the note and write the evidence on it." WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to place and justify notes. Point out the remaining questions on relative speed and safety, and mark them as 'Lesson 8' and 'Lesson 9'. Remind the class of the two KICD questions: "How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body?" and ask which part of acceleration they now know.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board tracking: showing questions answered and questions still open makes the learning journey visible and gives purpose to the next lessons, keeping learners focused on the driving question about describing and predicting the overtake.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: sticky notes include evidence (a number or graph feature) and not just a statement; new questions are linked to relative speed or safety; learners can say which earlier question the new evidence answers. Record the number of learners who linked evidence to questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update their class overtaking model (annotated diagram plus graphs). Individually they add to their model: (1) B's v-t graph labelled with 'gradient = 2 m/s^2' on 0-5 s and 'gradient = 0' on 5-7.5 s; (2) 'area = 125 m + 75 m = 200 m'; (3) A's graph labelled '20 m/s, area = 150 m'; (4) a note 'B gains 200 - 150 = 50 m'. They add a small inset for the braking matatu: 'a = -2 m/s^2, stopping distance 100 m'. Then they write a two-sentence statement on how gradient and area help describe and predict the overtake, and mark one idea they are still unsure of.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take out your model from Lesson 6. Add what we have learned today. Use different colours for gradient and area." Give WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before asking learners to start writing. Circulate and check that units are present (m/s^2, m). Cold-call 2 learners to read their two-sentence statements. Close by saying: "We know B travels 200 m and A 150 m. In Lesson 8 we ask: how fast does A seem to move from B, and what happens with the oncoming lorry L?" Collect models for review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: adding gradient and area to the model converts a picture of the overtake into a quantitative tool. Learners see how each new piece of evidence improves their ability to describe and predict motion.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: model contains correct labels for acceleration (2 m/s^2), distances (200 m, 150 m), gain (50 m) and the matatu (-2 m/s^2, 100 m); units are included; learners state at least one remaining uncertainty. Use the exit statement to decide which learners need support with trapezium areas or the sign of acceleration at the start of Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners could find a gradient from two points and explain what it means without prompting? Who confused the gradient (acceleration) with the height of the line (velocity)? How many learners split B's area into a trapezium and a rectangle by themselves? Were the table checks convincing? Did learners show that deceleration 2 m/s^2 means a = -2 m/s^2? What will I change in Lesson 8 to build from the 50 m gain to relative speed?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that Car B's velocity-time line slopes upward from 20 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s, then stays flat to 7.5 s; Car A's line is flat at 20 m/s; the braking matatu's line slopes downward from 20 m/s to 0 in 10 s. The areas under the graphs matched the split-time table.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration (B: 2 m/s^2; matatu: -2 m/s^2, deceleration 2 m/s^2) and the area under the graph gives distance travelled (B: 125 + 75 = 200 m; A: 150 m; matatu: 100 m).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that Car B travels 50 m more than Car A during the overtake because it sped up at 2 m/s^2, and that velocity-time graphs let us describe and predict the motion of the cars on the Naivasha highway using gradient and area.

LESSONS.title: Relative Speed: Why Does the Overtaken Car Look Slow?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: relative speed, same direction, opposite direction, viewpoint, closing speed, overtaking car B, overtaken car A, oncoming lorry L, velocity-time graph, area under graph

slo.purpose: Learners determine the relative speed of two bodies moving in the same direction (subtract speeds) and in opposite directions (add speeds), always stating the viewpoint, and use it to explain why overtaken car A looks slow from overtaking car B even though both speedometers read high.
slo.knowledge: Relative speed of two bodies moving in the same direction is the difference of their speeds; in opposite directions it is the sum of their speeds. The viewpoint must be stated (e.g. 'B relative to A'). B relative to A grows from 0 m/s at t = 0 to 10 m/s (36 km/h) at t = 5 s and then stays at 10 m/s. B and oncoming lorry L close at 30 + 20 = 50 m/s (180 km/h). The extra distance B gains on A (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 35, 45, 50 m) is the area under B's relative velocity graph: 1/2 x 5 x 10 = 25 m plus 10 x 2.5 = 25 m, total 50 m.
slo.skills: Calculating relative speed; converting between km/h and m/s (divide or multiply by 3.6); reading the B-minus-A column of the split-time table; drawing and interpreting a relative velocity-time graph; finding area under a graph (triangle and rectangle); communicating reasoning from a stated viewpoint. NGSS SEPs: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how everyday road observations can be explained with numbers; precision in stating viewpoints and units; responsibility and road safety awareness when thinking about overtaking on Kenyan roads; respect for others' reasoning during discussion.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? 2. How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body? (Lesson 8 extends question 1: velocity from one body's viewpoint is found by combining the velocities of two bodies; the acceleration of B from Lesson 3 explains why relative speed grows from 0 to 10 m/s.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 3 and 7 gave the velocities of A (20 m/s), B (20 to 30 m/s, a = 2 m/s^2) and L (-20 m/s) and the distances from areas under graphs. Lesson 8 answers the puzzle from Lesson 1: how can two fast vehicles look slow relative to each other? It supplies the relative speeds (10 m/s and 50 m/s) that Lesson 9 will use to judge whether the overtake is safe.
slo.safetyNotes: This is a classroom paper-and-graph lesson. If learners act out relative motion in the corridor or field, walk slowly in marked lanes, keep clear of doors and roads, and never run towards each other. Remind learners never to judge overtaking distances on a real road from a classroom rule; Kenyan road safety rules and a driver's full attention always apply.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the Naivasha highway clip: both speedometers show high speeds (72 km/h and up to 108 km/h), yet car A looks slow from car B. They first predict relative speeds, then gather evidence from the split-time table (B minus A column: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 35, 45, 50 m) and by calculating B relative to A and B and L closing speeds. They explain the results with a relative velocity-time graph whose area equals the 50 m gained, update the Driving Question Board with new questions about safety, and revise their class model, adding relative speed as a link between the speedometers and what the drivers see.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners re-watch the Naivasha clip (or hear it described) and look at the speedometer facts at t = 0: A and B both show 72 km/h (20 m/s). In pairs they predict and write: (a) How fast does A seem to move from Wanjiru's seat in car B at t = 0? (b) How fast does A seem to move when B has reached 108 km/h? (c) How fast does oncoming lorry L (72 km/h towards Naivasha) seem to approach car B when B is at 108 km/h? They record the prediction with a short reason in their notebooks and draw a quick sketch with arrows for direction.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Imagine you are Achieng in the back seat of car B watching car A through the windscreen. Does A look fast or slow? Write your prediction before we calculate anything.' Give 2 minutes of individual writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What do you think happens to how fast A seems to move as B speeds up?' Cold-call 4 pairs and record predictions on the board without judging them as right or wrong. Say: 'Hold on to your prediction; we will test it with the numbers from the split-time table.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-and-record (Think-Pair-Share): committing to a prediction in writing makes learners aware of their prior ideas, such as 'a fast car must look fast', so that the later evidence creates real conceptual conflict and is remembered.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: predictions written down by every learner; sketches with direction arrows; reasons that mention viewpoint or speed difference. Note how many of the 4 cold-called pairs predict that A looks fast from B at t = 0 (a common misconception) and tally predictions on the board for comparison at the end of the lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 with the split-time table. Step 1: Study the B minus A column (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 35, 45, 50 m at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7.5 s) and calculate how much extra distance B gains each second: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 in the first five seconds, then 10 m per second after t = 5 s (25 to 35 to 45). Step 2: Calculate B relative to A as the difference of velocities at each time: t = 0, 0 m/s; t = 1, 22 - 20 = 2; t = 2, 4; t = 3, 6; t = 4, 8; t = 5, 10 m/s; and 10 m/s afterwards. Convert 10 m/s to 36 km/h. Step 3: Calculate the closing speed of B and oncoming lorry L when B is at 30 m/s: 30 + 20 = 50 m/s = 180 km/h. Step 4: Role play in the corridor with two learners walking in the same direction at different slow speeds, then towards each other, noticing how fast the gap changes.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the table and circulate. Say: 'Look at the B minus A column. What does the gap-gaining pattern tell you about how fast B is moving relative to A?' Prompt with: 'At t = 0 both speedometers show 72 km/h. What is B relative to A at that moment?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Ask: 'Why do we subtract the speeds for A and B but add them for B and L?' and cold-call 3 groups. Remind groups to write the viewpoint each time, e.g. 'B relative to A = 30 - 20 = 10 m/s'. Use the corridor demonstration with two learners: walking the same way at 1 m/s and 2 m/s, then walking towards each other, and ask the class to describe the speed at which the gap changes.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data pattern analysis with a structured table: learners compute a new column (relative speed) from given data and look for patterns, which builds the rule 'same direction subtract, opposite direction add' from evidence rather than being told it. The physical walking demonstration gives a concrete, embodied model of the rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that groups: calculate B relative to A as 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 10 m/s correctly; write the viewpoint in every statement; use 72 km/h = 20 m/s and 108 km/h = 30 m/s correctly; compute 50 m/s and 180 km/h for B and L. Common errors to watch: subtracting for opposite directions, forgetting units, or giving 100 m/s because both are written as positive speeds. Tick off each group on a checklist as they complete each step.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their calculations to build a written explanation in the format Claim-Evidence-Reasoning. Claim: car A looks slow from car B because their relative speed is small. Evidence: at t = 0 B relative to A = 0 m/s; after t = 5 s it is only 10 m/s (36 km/h); B gains 50 m in 7.5 s. Reasoning: both cars move in the same direction so we subtract speeds. They then draw a velocity-time graph of B relative to A (t on the x-axis, 1 cm = 1 s; relative velocity on the y-axis) rising as a straight line from 0 to 10 m/s at 5 s, then flat to 7.5 s. They find the area: triangle 1/2 x 5 x 10 = 25 m plus rectangle 10 x 2.5 = 25 m, total 50 m, and match it to the last row of the B minus A column (50 m = 20 m gap + 5 m + 5 m + 20 m). They also explain why oncoming lorry L is dangerous: closing speed 50 m/s (180 km/h).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use the sentence frame: From the viewpoint of ___, the other vehicle seems to move at ___ because ___.' Ask: 'The speedometer says 108 km/h in car B, yet A looks slow. How can both be true?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to share their reasoning. Ask: 'Which slope on your relative graph tells us B's relative speed is growing? What does the gradient 2 m/s^2 from Lesson 3 have to do with it?' Guide learners to see that the gradient of the relative graph equals B's acceleration because A has no acceleration. Ask: 'Why does the area under the relative graph give 50 m, and where have you seen 50 m before?' Ask learners to compare to their predictions from the Predict Phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a graphical model: learners link a verbal explanation to numbers and to a graph; using the area under the relative velocity graph connects Lesson 7's area idea with the B minus A column, which strengthens the link between multiple representations (table, graph, words).
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for explanations that (1) state the viewpoint, (2) subtract for same direction and add for opposite, (3) use the 10 m/s (36 km/h) and 50 m/s (180 km/h) values correctly, and (4) show the graph with correct axes, labels and scale (1 cm = 1 s). Check that the area calculation gives 25 + 25 = 50 m. Ask 5 learners to explain one step aloud; note who can explain why relative speed starts at 0 when both speedometers show 72 km/h.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board. They sort existing question cards into 'answered', 'partly answered' and 'still open'. They place answered cards such as 'Why does A look slow from B?' with a note: 'B relative to A is only 10 m/s (36 km/h) in the same direction; it was 0 at t = 0.' They write new questions on sticky notes, e.g. 'Is 150 m of space left when B pulls in enough?', 'How much road does B need in total with lorry L approaching?', 'What if the lorry had been closer?' and 'How do we know the total time of 7.5 s is safe?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk to the board in your groups and decide which of our questions we can now answer using relative speed.' Ask: 'Which questions are still open, and which of them need us to combine distance, time and relative speed?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking suggestions. Cold-call 3 groups to read one answered and one new question. Point out the new safety questions and say: 'These will lead us into the next lesson, where we decide whether the overtake is safe.' Add a card: 'How can we use relative speed to describe and predict the overtake?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board tracking: sorting and generating questions makes learning progress visible, links this lesson's evidence to the main driving question, and gives learners ownership of what to investigate next.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 3 new learner questions refer to relative speed, total road needed or lorry L, and that answered cards include evidence (a number and the viewpoint). Observe whether learners can explain why a card moves from 'open' to 'answered'. Note groups who write only vague questions such as 'How fast?' and prompt them to add a viewpoint or unit.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model of the overtaking (a labelled diagram with a timeline and graphs). They add: (1) arrows for A (20 m/s), B (20 to 30 m/s) and L (-20 m/s) with positive direction towards Nakuru; (2) a 'relative speed' box: B relative to A = 0 to 10 m/s (36 km/h) by subtraction; B and L closing speed 50 m/s (180 km/h) by addition; (3) the relative velocity-time graph with the area 50 m; (4) a short caption: 'A looks slow from B because the relative speed is only 10 m/s, even though both speedometers read high.' They then compare with their initial predictions, correct any that were wrong and write one sentence on what changed in their thinking.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Update your model so that someone who was not in class could understand why A looks slow from B.' Circulate and ask: 'Where on your model can I see the viewpoint? Where is the 50 m? Which part shows the lorry closing at 180 km/h?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to present one addition to the model. Ask: 'What does the model not yet tell us?' to lead towards the safety margin in Lesson 9. Return to the tally of predictions from the Predict Phase and ask learners to say how their ideas changed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding relative speed to the existing model lets learners integrate new knowledge with earlier ideas (velocity, acceleration, graphs, areas) and see how the parts explain the phenomenon as one system.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that include: viewpoint statements, correct values 10 m/s and 50 m/s with km/h conversions (36 km/h and 180 km/h), the 0 to 10 m/s growth, the 50 m gained, and a caption explaining why A looks slow. Use a 3-point checklist (viewpoint, rule for same/opposite direction, correct numbers) and record how many groups meet all three. Exit ticket: 'Write one sentence that explains why A looks slow from B.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still believed that 'a fast speedometer reading means the other car must look fast', and what evidence changed their mind? Did learners state the viewpoint every time (e.g. 'B relative to A')? Did anyone add speeds for the same direction or subtract them for opposite directions, and how did the corridor demonstration or the graph help correct this? Were the km/h and m/s conversions secure? Which questions on the DQB show learners are ready to combine time, distance and relative speed in Lesson 9? Note any adjustments to pacing, grouping or materials for next time.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that at t = 0 both car A and car B show 72 km/h (20 m/s), yet B gains 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 35, 45 and 50 m on A at t = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 7.5 s, and oncoming lorry L moves towards them at 20 m/s.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that relative speed is found by subtracting speeds for bodies moving in the same direction (B relative to A = 30 - 20 = 10 m/s = 36 km/h, growing from 0 at t = 0 to 10 m/s at t = 5 s) and by adding speeds for bodies moving in opposite directions (B and L: 30 + 20 = 50 m/s = 180 km/h), always stating the viewpoint. The area under B's relative velocity graph, 25 + 25 = 50 m, gives the extra distance B gains.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Car A looks slow from car B because they move in the same direction, so their relative speed is only 10 m/s (36 km/h) and was 0 at the start, even though both speedometers read high. The oncoming lorry looks very fast from B because it closes at 50 m/s (180 km/h), which is why the overtake needs careful checking in the next lesson.

LESSONS.title: Applying Linear Motion: Is Wanjiru's Overtake Safe?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: overtaking, relative speed, safety margin, total road needed, velocity-time graph, area under graph, oncoming lorry, Naivasha highway

slo.purpose: Learners combine time, distance and relative speed to decide whether the overtake on the Nairobi-Nakuru highway is safe, using the total road needed (350 m) and the safety margin in metres and seconds.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) state that B needs 7.5 s to complete the overtake, during which B travels 200 m, A travels 150 m and oncoming lorry L travels 150 m; (2) explain that B and L together use 200 + 150 = 350 m of the road; (3) find the safety margin as 500 - 350 = 150 m and convert it to time using closing speed 50 m/s (150 / 50 = 3.0 s); (4) apply the same method to the what-if case of a lorry 400 m away (margin 50 m, 1.0 s, unsafe).
slo.skills: Calculating with a = (v - u)/t and areas under a velocity-time graph (Lesson 7); using relative speed from a stated viewpoint (Lesson 8); organising multi-step calculations in a table; making and justifying a safety decision with evidence (NGSS SEP: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Engaging in Argument from Evidence).
slo.attitudes: Learners show responsibility and care for road safety, respect for evidence-based decisions, and curiosity and perseverance when combining several ideas to solve a real problem.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? 2. How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body? (Learners use both, v = displacement/time and a = (v - u)/t, as tools in the safety decision.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 3, 7 and 8 gave us the tools: velocity and acceleration, areas under velocity-time graphs, and relative speed. Lesson 9 applies them to answer the real question behind the phenomenon: can Wanjiru overtake before the oncoming lorry arrives? It prepares learners for Lesson 10, where they present the full model and answer the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: All work is classroom-based, using video, paper and calculators. Do NOT ask learners to measure speeds on a real road. Use the lesson to discuss safe overtaking: never overtake when an oncoming vehicle is close, on bends or on hills. Move desks aside for the role-play and keep walkways clear.

LESSONS.overview: Learners revisit the overtaking clip near Naivasha and predict whether Wanjiru's Subaru (Car B) can overtake Mr Kamau's Axio (Car A) safely when Mr Otieno's lorry (L) is 500 m ahead. They rebuild the evidence from earlier lessons (B: 20 to 30 m/s in 5 s, a = 2 m/s^2; B travels 200 m, A 150 m, L 150 m in 7.5 s; relative speed 10 m/s for B relative to A and 50 m/s closing speed for B and L). They then calculate the total road needed (350 m), the safety margin (150 m, 3.0 s) and test a what-if where the lorry is only 400 m away (margin 50 m, 1.0 s, unsafe). The lesson closes by adding the safety decision to the DQB and to the class model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners re-watch the Naivasha overtaking clip (or view the teacher's description card) and individually write a prediction in their notebooks: 'Is Wanjiru's overtake safe when the oncoming lorry is 500 m from B at t = 0? What do we need to know to decide?' They sketch a simple road diagram showing B, A and L, then pair up and compare. They list which quantities they think matter (time, distances, speeds).
framework.teacherMoves: Play the clip twice, pausing at t = 0 when both cars show 72 km/h. Say: 'Wanjiru is about to speed up. Mr Otieno's lorry is 500 m ahead, coming towards us. Would YOU pull out? Write Yes, No or Not sure, and one reason.' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds of silent writing. Then cold-call 4 learners from different parts of the room: 'Tell us your decision and what information you would want.' Record the wanted information on the board as a list (time to overtake, distance of B, distance of lorry, speeds). Do not confirm any answer yet. Say: 'By the end of today we will decide using numbers, not feelings.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Revise: committing to a written prediction and a list of needed information exposes preconceptions (e.g. 'fast cars are always safe', 'only B's speed matters'). Learners will later revise their prediction against calculated evidence, making the change in their thinking visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) learners who write a Yes/No/Not sure decision with a reason; (b) whether the list of needed information includes the lorry's speed and the time or distance of the overtake; (c) misconceptions such as 'only B's speed matters' or 'the lorry is far, so it is safe'. Note names on a checklist for targeted questioning later.

framework.learnerExperience: Working in groups of four, learners complete an evidence table using the data from earlier lessons and the split-time table. Roles: Reader, Calculator, Recorder, Checker. Step 1: from the v-t graph for B, find the acceleration (30 - 20)/5 = 2 m/s^2 and areas: trapezium (20 + 30)/2 x 5 = 125 m plus rectangle 30 x 2.5 = 75 m, giving B = 200 m in 7.5 s. Step 2: A travels 20 x 7.5 = 150 m; lorry L travels 20 x 7.5 = 150 m (velocity -20 m/s, distance is a magnitude). Step 3: check the relative distance B minus A = 200 - 150 = 50 m = 20 m gap + 5 m (A length) + 5 m (B length) + 20 m finishing gap. Step 4: calculate total road used by B and L together: 200 + 150 = 350 m. Step 5: find the road left: 500 - 350 = 150 m. Step 6: using closing speed 30 + 20 = 50 m/s, convert to time: 150 / 50 = 3.0 s. They label a road diagram at t = 0 and t = 7.5 s with these distances.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the split-time table and a blank evidence table. Circulate and ask: 'Which lesson's tool are you using here, velocity, areas or relative speed?' and 'Why do we ADD the distances of B and L but SUBTRACT the distances of B and A?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds after each question before taking answers. For groups stuck on Step 4, prompt: 'Both vehicles are using the same strip of road, coming from opposite ends. Draw them at t = 0 and t = 7.5 s. How much of the 500 m have they eaten up together?' After 15 minutes, cold-call 3 groups to report one row each of the table. Check the 7.5 s row of the split-time table (B 200 m, A 150 m, B minus A = 50 m) against learners' answers. Remind them the safe-overtake calculation uses only the numbers established in the clip; no other values are to be invented.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Data Table with Role Rotation: breaking the problem into labelled steps lets learners connect three prior tools (acceleration, area under the v-t graph, relative speed) into one chain of reasoning, and the diagram links abstract numbers to the physical road near Naivasha. Cross-checking with the split-time table builds confidence in the model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners correctly get 125 + 75 = 200 m; state A = 150 m and L = 150 m; add rather than subtract to get 350 m; compute 150 m and 3.0 s with units; and can explain 50 m as 20 + 5 + 5 + 20. Common errors to note: using 72 km/h without conversion, using -20 m/s in a distance sum (giving 50 m), dividing 150 by 30 or 20 instead of 50, forgetting the car lengths.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group writes a 'Safety Verdict' on a half sheet of paper using the claim-evidence-reasoning format: Claim (Is the overtake safe with the lorry 500 m away?), Evidence (350 m used, 150 m left, 3.0 s), Reasoning (why the margin is positive and what 3.0 s means for Mr Otieno and Wanjiru). Then the class tests the what-if: the lorry is only 400 m away at t = 0. Groups calculate: road used is still 350 m, margin 400 - 350 = 50 m, time 50 / 50 = 1.0 s, and decide this is unsafe, explaining that a 1.0 s gap is far too small for drivers to react or brake. They also explain, in their own words, why both cars can show high speedometer readings yet A looks slow from B (relative speed 10 m/s, 36 km/h), while the lorry seems very fast from B (50 m/s, 180 km/h). They revisit their Predict Phase decision and revise it.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the CER structure once with a sentence frame on the board: 'I claim ___ because the evidence shows ___, which means ___.' Then say: 'Now change one number. The lorry is 400 m away. Predict first: safe or unsafe? Show with fingers.' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, then ask groups to calculate. Cold-call 5 learners to give one step each of the what-if solution: road used, margin in metres, closing speed, margin in seconds, verdict. Ask: 'Why does the 350 m not change when the lorry is closer?' and 'What would you say to a driver who says 1.0 s is enough?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds before taking responses. Stress the conventions: say 'overtaking car B', 'overtaken car A' and 'oncoming lorry L', and always state the viewpoint when using relative speed. Link to the key inquiry questions: ask which calculation used velocity and which used acceleration.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a what-if (variable change): changing only one variable (lorry distance) isolates cause and effect, helping learners see that safety depends on the margin, not on how fast the cars look. Writing reasoning in sentences forces them to connect numbers to the physical meaning of the overtake.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check verdicts for: a clear claim; use of 150 m and 3.0 s as evidence; the what-if numbers 50 m and 1.0 s; the explanation that 1.0 s is unsafe. Success indicators: learners use 'relative speed of B relative to A is 10 m/s' and 'closing speed of B and L is 50 m/s' correctly with viewpoint. Ask 3 learners to restate the verdict without notes. Misconception check: 'Because B is faster than L, there is no danger.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. In their groups, they pick questions already on the board about 'how long does it take', 'how far do the cars travel' and 'is it safe' and mark which ones they can now answer with evidence (7.5 s; B 200 m, A 150 m, L 150 m; 350 m used; margin 150 m or 3.0 s). They write answers on sticky notes with the data source (for example, 'area under v-t graph, Lesson 7'). They add new questions, such as 'What if B accelerated faster?', 'What if the road were wet?', 'What if the lorry was heavier or faster?', and 'What is the minimum safe distance for the lorry?' and place them on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Let us look at our board. Which questions can we now answer, and which have we only partly answered?' Ask 4 learners (cold-call) to bring a note to the board and read their answer with the evidence. WAIT TIME: 10 seconds before asking, 'What new question did today raise for you?' Group questions by type: calculation, safety, and beyond-the-data (road conditions, driver reaction). Mark the beyond-the-data questions as ideas for discussion in Lesson 10 only. Reinforce: 'We use only the data from our clip; the new questions help us think about what else we would need to measure.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Tracking: moving from questions to evidence-based answers shows learners their own progress and keeps the whole class oriented toward the driving question. Sorting new questions identifies the limits of the model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether sticky notes give correct values with units and cite the source (graph, table or calculation). Check that at least one question from each group links to safety or relative speed. Indicators of progress: learners who previously asked only 'how fast?' now ask about margins, time and conditions.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners add a 'Safety Decision' panel to their class model of the overtake. The panel contains: (1) a labelled road diagram at t = 0 and t = 7.5 s showing A, B and L with the distances 150 m, 200 m, 150 m; (2) a small velocity-time graph for B (trapezium and rectangle, area 200 m) and A (horizontal line at 20 m/s, area 150 m); (3) a one-line calculation chain: 200 + 150 = 350 m; 500 - 350 = 150 m; 150 / 50 = 3.0 s; (4) the what-if result (400 m gives 50 m, 1.0 s, unsafe); (5) a sentence stating the safety rule they have developed: 'An overtake is safe only when the distance to the oncoming vehicle is greater than the road used by the overtaking car and the oncoming vehicle, with a good time margin.' They compare their panel with a partner and improve it. Then they complete the Summary Table prompt in their books.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model must let someone who was not in our class decide if Wanjiru can safely overtake. What must they see?' Give 10 minutes of silent individual work, then 5 minutes of partner critique with the prompt: 'Find one thing that is clear and one thing that could be clearer.' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds when asking for share-outs; cold-call 3 learners to read their safety rule. Highlight good models on the board. Close with an exit ticket: 'A lorry is 450 m away at t = 0. Using the same overtake (350 m used, closing speed 50 m/s), find the margin in metres and seconds, and say if you would overtake.' (Answer: 100 m, 2.0 s; learners justify their decision using the evidence.)
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Peer Critique: adding a decision panel connects graphs, calculations and diagrams into one coherent explanation, and peer critique helps learners refine their reasoning and communicate it clearly. The exit ticket tests transfer to a new number.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model checklist: correct distances (150 m, 200 m, 150 m); 350 m total; margin 150 m and 3.0 s; what-if 50 m and 1.0 s; labelled axes and scales (1 cm = 1 s on x-axis); a safety rule in words. Exit ticket indicators: correct 450 - 350 = 100 m; 100 / 50 = 2.0 s; a justified decision referring to the margin. Learners who miss the exit ticket receive a short follow-up with the evidence table at the start of Lesson 10.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Which learners could chain the three tools (acceleration, area, relative speed) without prompts, and which needed the diagram? Did learners confuse adding distances of B and L (opposite directions) with subtracting distances of B and A (same direction)? Did anyone mix up m/s and km/h in the closing speed? Was the 3.0 s margin meaningful to learners, and did they appreciate why 1.0 s is unsafe? Were all learners able to take part in the discussions, including quieter ones? What evidence from the exit ticket will you use to plan the review at the start of Lesson 10, where learners present the final model and answer the driving question and the two KICD key inquiry questions?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What we observed: In the Naivasha clip, overtaking car B took 7.5 s to pass overtaken car A. In that time B travelled 200 m, A travelled 150 m and oncoming lorry L travelled 150 m. B gained 50 m on A.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What we learned: We can combine acceleration (a = 2 m/s^2), areas under velocity-time graphs and relative speed to decide if an overtake is safe. B and L together use 350 m of road. The safety margin is the distance to the lorry minus 350 m, and dividing by the closing speed of 50 m/s gives the margin in seconds.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How this explains the phenomenon: With the lorry 500 m away, the margin is 150 m, or 3.0 s, so Wanjiru's overtake is safe. If the lorry were only 400 m away, the margin would be 50 m, or 1.0 s, which is unsafe. Both cars can have high speedometer readings, but safety depends on relative speeds and the road available, not on speedometer readings alone.
