LESSONS.title: Final Model and Answer to the Driving Question: Overtaking on the Naivasha Highway
LESSONS.aresKeywords: overtaking, distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, relative speed, displacement-time graph, velocity-time graph, gradient, area under graph, safety margin, final explanation

slo.purpose: Learners synthesise everything from Lessons 1-9 into one complete model of the overtaking event (annotated graphs plus calculations), present it, and use it to answer the driving question and the two KICD key inquiry questions. No new skill is taught.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) explain that velocity is the rate of change of displacement with time, a vector with direction shown by sign (Car A +20 m/s, oncoming lorry L -20 m/s); (2) explain that acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = (v - u)/t, so overtaking car B has a = (30 - 20)/5 = 2 m/s^2; (3) use the area under the velocity-time graph to show B travels 200 m and A travels 150 m in 7.5 s; (4) use relative speed (10 m/s for B relative to A, 50 m/s closing speed for B and L) to explain why A looks slow from B; (5) use the 350 m of road needed and the lorry 500 m away to show a 150 m (3.0 s) safety margin.
slo.skills: Science and Engineering Practices: Developing and using models (completing, presenting and revising the final model); Constructing explanations (writing the Final Explanation using claim-evidence-reasoning); Analysing and interpreting data (checking the model against the split-time table); Engaging in argument from evidence (peer critique of models); Using mathematics and computational thinking (calculations of velocity, acceleration, area and relative speed). Core competencies: critical thinking and problem solving, communication and collaboration.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of mathematics in keeping Kenyan road users safe, show respect for peers' ideas during model critique, display honesty in comparing the Lesson 1 predictions with the final model, and value responsible road use (Values: responsibility, integrity, respect).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do you determine the velocity of a moving body? 2. How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body? Driving question: How can we use distance, time, speed, velocity and graphs to describe and predict how one car overtakes another on a Kenyan road?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the culminating lesson. In Lesson 1 learners saw the overtaking clip near Naivasha and were puzzled that both speedometers looked high yet A looked slow from B. Lessons 2-9 gave them tools: definitions (L2), velocity and acceleration calculations (L3), displacement-time graphs (L4-5), velocity-time graphs and areas (L6-7), relative speed (L8) and the safe-overtake decision (L9). Here they pull all of it together, compare with their Lesson 1 model, close out the Driving Question Board and answer the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: Classroom-based lesson; keep walkways clear during gallery walks and presentations. Do not encourage learners to imitate overtaking or measure speeds on a real road. Emphasise that real overtaking is dangerous and that the numbers show why drivers must leave a large margin, especially when oncoming vehicles such as lorry L are near.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the Naivasha highway clip where Wanjiru in white Subaru B overtakes Mr Kamau's blue Toyota Axio A while Mr Otieno's lorry L approaches. In groups they complete a final model made of annotated velocity-time and displacement-time graphs, the split-time table and key calculations: B accelerates from 20 to 30 m/s in 5 s (a = 2 m/s^2); B travels 200 m while A travels 150 m in 7.5 s; B gains 50 m (20 m gap + 5 m + 5 m + 20 m gap); B relative to A is only 10 m/s (36 km/h) while B and L close at 50 m/s (180 km/h); the lorry started 500 m away and B and L cover 350 m together, leaving 150 m or 3.0 s. Learners compare this with their Lesson 1 prediction model, present to peers, complete the Driving Question Board by marking each question answered with evidence, and write a Final Explanation answering the driving question and the two KICD questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners re-watch the overtaking clip (Nairobi-Nakuru highway near Naivasha) and, individually, take out their Lesson 1 prediction (how long and how far the overtake takes). On a half sheet they write a new prediction: 'If lorry L were as far away as in the clip, would Wanjiru's overtake be safe, and what numbers would prove it?' They then pair up and compare their Lesson 1 sketch with what they now think, and mark one idea they are keeping and one they would change.
framework.teacherMoves: Play the clip twice with sound off. Say: 'Look back at your Lesson 1 prediction. Now, before we open any notes, write what numbers you would need to decide if Wanjiru's overtake is safe.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds in silence before pairs talk. Cold-call 4 learners: 'What is one thing you predicted in Lesson 1 that you can now check with a number?' Record responses on the board under 'Then' and leave space for 'Now'. Do not confirm answers yet; say: 'Hold that thought, we will test it with our evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction revisited (Think-Pair-Share): returning to a recorded prediction makes learners aware of how their thinking has changed and gives a concrete baseline for the later L1-versus-final model comparison.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: learners naming quantities needed (time, distance travelled by B and A, relative speed, distance to lorry L); learners referencing specific Lesson 1 statements; learners who still say 'A looks slow because it is slow' (flag for support during the Observe phase). Tally on the clipboard how many of 4 cold-calls mention distance to the lorry.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 gather their evidence from Lessons 1-9: the split-time table (t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7.5 s with B distance, A distance and B minus A), their velocity-time graph of B (trapezium 0-5 s, rectangle 5-7.5 s) and A (horizontal line at 20 m/s), and their relative speed and safety margin calculations. Using A3 paper and graph paper (1 cm = 1 s on the x-axis), they build a final model with four panels: (1) velocity-time graphs of A and B with gradient 2 m/s^2 labelled and areas 125 m + 75 = 200 m for B and 20 x 7.5 = 150 m for A; (2) a scale road diagram showing the 20 m gap, 5 m car lengths and 20 m finishing gap, totalling 50 m gained by 7.5 s (level at t = 5 s, B's rear passes A's front at 5.5 s); (3) relative speed panel (B relative to A rising from 0 to 10 m/s = 36 km/h; B and L closing at 30 + 20 = 50 m/s = 180 km/h; lorry velocity -20 m/s); (4) safety panel (200 + 150 = 350 m, 500 - 350 = 150 m, 150/50 = 3.0 s). Each group checks that every number matches the split-time table.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Say: 'Every number on your model must be traceable to the table or to a graph. Show me where 200 m comes from.' Ask groups: 'What does the gradient of this line tell us? What does the area tell us?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question before prompting. Cold-call 3 groups to point to the table row (t = 5 s: B 125 m, A 100 m, gained 25 m) that matches their milestone. Prompt groups missing a direction sign: 'Which direction is positive? What sign does lorry L get?' Do not give answers; redirect to Lesson 3 (velocity and acceleration calculations) and Lesson 7 (gradient and area) work.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence mapping with a consensus model: learners assemble multiple representations (table, graph, diagram, calculation) of the same event and must reconcile them, which builds understanding that these are different views of one motion.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check: gradient labelled 2 m/s^2 with working (30 - 20)/5; areas correctly split into trapezium (20+30)/2 x 5 = 125 m and rectangle 30 x 2.5 = 75 m; A = 150 m; 50 m gained decomposed as 20 + 5 + 5 + 20; lorry velocity negative; units (m/s, km/h, m, s) present. Note groups with arithmetic or sign errors and give a targeted question, not the answer.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group presents its model in a 3-minute gallery presentation (one speaker, one pointer, one timekeeper, one recorder) while other groups rotate. Presenters must explain why Car A looks slow from Car B even though both speedometers show high values (72 km/h and up to 108 km/h), and why the manoeuvre is safe in the clip but would not be if lorry L were 400 m away. Visitors use a critique card: 'One thing the model explains well; one question; one suggestion.' Afterwards learners individually write the Final Explanation in claim-evidence-reasoning form: Claim answering the driving question; Evidence using at least four numbers from the model; Reasoning linking velocity (rate of change of displacement), acceleration (rate of change of velocity), graphs (gradient and area) and relative speed. They also write short answers to the two KICD questions: how to determine velocity (displacement divided by time, or gradient of a displacement-time graph) and how to determine acceleration ((v - u)/t, or gradient of a velocity-time graph).
framework.teacherMoves: Set norms: 'We critique the model, not the people.' During presentations say: 'Presenters, tell us the viewpoint when you give a relative speed: B relative to A, or B and L together.' After each rotation ask: 'Which part of the model did you find most convincing, and why?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before accepting responses. Cold-call 5 learners across groups to restate in their own words why A looks slow from B (relative speed only 10 m/s in the same direction, starting from 0 when acceleration begins) compared with the 50 m/s closing speed with L. For the what-if, ask: 'If lorry L were 400 m away, what margin remains?' Expect 400 - 350 = 50 m, 1.0 s, unsafe. Provide the CER sentence frames to learners who need them: 'I claim... The evidence is... This shows that...'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with peer argumentation: requiring numerical evidence and explicit reasoning, then having peers challenge it, pushes learners from describing what happened to explaining why, and uses their model as an argument.
framework.formativeAssessment: Rubric (0-3) for the Final Explanation: correct claim; at least four accurate numbers (a = 2 m/s^2, 200 m vs 150 m, 7.5 s, 10 m/s, 50 m/s, 150 m / 3.0 s); reasoning that links relative speed to the appearance of slow motion; correct KICD answers (velocity = displacement/time; a = (v - u)/t). Observable errors to flag: using the sum instead of the difference of speeds for same-direction motion; confusing distance and displacement; forgetting that the road must be shared with L (350 m). Collect exit sheets to target follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1 (questions such as 'How long does overtaking take?', 'How far do the cars travel?', 'Why does A look slow from B?', 'Is it safe with the lorry coming?'). In their groups they take each question card, decide whether it is Answered, Partly answered or Still open, and write on a sticky note the evidence (a number, graph or lesson) that answers it, then place the note on the board. They add new questions that arise, for example: 'What if the road were wet?', 'What if Car A also sped up?' or 'What changes with a slope or a bend?'. The class reads the completed board and decides the final answer to the driving question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take one question from Lesson 1. Show the class the evidence that answers it.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 6 learners (one per question category: time, distance, speed, velocity/acceleration, relative speed, safety). Ask: 'Which question could we not have answered without graphs? Which needed relative speed?' For open questions, say: 'Good questions we cannot yet answer are the start of new science; we leave them here for future lessons, for example how road conditions would change these numbers.' Do not add new content; note that wet-road braking and bends need ideas outside this sub-strand.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question-tracking (DQB closure): linking each original question to specific evidence shows learners the arc of their learning and legitimises remaining questions as next steps.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe: each note cites specific evidence (e.g., 'Lesson 7: area under B's graph = 200 m'); learners correctly classify questions; at least one new, testable question per group. Record how many of the 6 cold-calls give an evidence-based response without teacher prompting.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners compare their Lesson 1 model (sketch/prediction with no numbers) with the final model side by side using a two-column table: 'Lesson 1 model' and 'Final model' with rows for time, distance, speed/velocity, acceleration, relative speed and safety. They highlight what changed and what stayed the same, then revise any part of their final model that still has an error after peer critique. Each learner writes a short Summary Table entry (what we observed, learned, explained) and a two-sentence answer to the driving question, for example: 'Using distance, time, velocity, acceleration and graphs, we find that B, accelerating at 2 m/s^2 to 30 m/s, takes 7.5 s and 200 m to overtake A, which travels 150 m at 20 m/s; because B relative to A is only 10 m/s, A looks slow; and since B and lorry L need 350 m of the 500 m, a 150 m (3.0 s) margin remains.' Finally, learners connect to their own lives by writing one road-safety message for a Kenyan driver or boda boda rider based on the numbers.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Place your Lesson 1 model next to your final model. What can your final model do that your first could not?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 4 learners to name one change and the evidence that caused it. Challenge: 'If Mr Kamau in Car A also sped up during the overtake, which part of your model would change?' Take 2 volunteers. Close by reading the driving question aloud and asking the class to give the one-sentence answer in chorus, then invite 3 learners to read their road-safety messages. Praise honest revision: 'Changing your model because of evidence is exactly what scientists do.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model comparison and revision (then-versus-now): explicit side-by-side comparison makes conceptual change visible and lets learners see mathematics as a tool to describe and predict, not just compute.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: Lesson 1 model correctly characterised (qualitative, no numbers or mixed up speed and relative speed); final model includes graphs with gradient and area, correct figures and units; the driving-question answer includes velocity, acceleration, relative speed and the safety margin; road-safety message is consistent with the data (for example, leave a large margin because closing speed with an oncoming lorry is 50 m/s = 180 km/h). Use a 4-level rubric (beginning, developing, secure, extending).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Which parts of the final model did learners complete without help, and which numbers (for example 350 m or 3.0 s) caused most errors? Did cold-calling reveal learners still thinking that A looks slow because it is slow? Compare Lesson 1 predictions with final explanations for at least five learners: how many now use relative speed correctly and state the viewpoint? Were the 10-15 second wait times observed, and did quieter learners contribute? Which open DQB questions could be the basis for the next sub-strand or an extension project? Note adjustments for the next class, including extra practice on gradient and area, and whether the Kenyan contexts (Naivasha highway, matatus, boda boda) supported engagement.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions:
Final Explanation: Overtaking on the Naivasha Highway. Driving question: How can we use distance, time, speed, velocity and graphs to describe and predict how one car overtakes another on a Kenyan road? Remember the clip near Naivasha: Wanjiru in the white Subaru (overtaking car B) passes Mr Kamau's blue Toyota Axio (overtaken car A) while Mr Otieno's lorry (oncoming lorry L) approaches from Nakuru. Take the direction towards Nakuru as positive. Answer every section in the space below each prompt. Show your working, write units with every answer, and use evidence from your graphs, your split-time table and your Driving Question Board. Use the words 'overtaking car B', 'overtaken car A' and 'oncoming lorry L', and always say whose viewpoint you are using when you talk about relative speed. Use the table below in Sections 2 to 4.

| t (s) | v of B (m/s) | B distance (m) | A distance (m) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 20 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 22 | 21 | 20 |
| 2 | 24 | 44 | 40 |
| 3 | 26 | 69 | 60 |
| 4 | 28 | 96 | 80 |
| 5 | 30 | 125 | 100 |
| 6 | 30 | 155 | 120 |
| 7 | 30 | 185 | 140 |
| 7.5 | 30 | 200 | 150 |

sections.title: Section 1: Describing the motion of each vehicle (KICD Question 1: How do you determine the velocity of a moving body?)
sections.prompt: Car A covers 150 m in 7.5 s, and the oncoming lorry L travels towards Naivasha, covering 150 m in the same 7.5 s. (a) Explain how you determine the velocity of a moving body, and say how velocity is different from speed. (b) Calculate the velocity of overtaken car A. (c) Convert the speedometer readings of 72 km/h and 108 km/h to m/s. (d) Find the velocity of oncoming lorry L and explain what its sign tells you.
sections.exemplar: (a) Velocity = displacement / time. You find how far the body has changed position in a straight line, in a stated direction, and divide by the time taken. Speed uses total distance (a scalar), but velocity uses displacement and direction (a vector), and the direction is shown by the sign. A speedometer shows speed only. (b) Car A: v = 150 m / 7.5 s = 20 m/s towards Nakuru, so +20 m/s. (c) Divide km/h by 3.6: 72 / 3.6 = 20 m/s and 108 / 3.6 = 30 m/s. (d) Oncoming lorry L: its speed is 150 m / 7.5 s = 20 m/s. It travels towards Naivasha, opposite to the positive direction (towards Nakuru), so its velocity is -20 m/s. The negative sign shows direction, not slowing down.

sections.title: Section 2: Acceleration from numbers and from a graph (KICD Question 2: How do you determine the acceleration of a moving body?)
sections.prompt: Use the table. (a) Explain how you determine the acceleration of a moving body and calculate the acceleration of overtaking car B while its velocity rises from its starting value to its final value. State the time it takes. (b) Sketch the velocity-time graph for car B from t = 0 to 7.5 s and for car A on the same axes. Use t (s) on the x-axis and v (m/s) on the y-axis. (c) Explain how the graph also gives the acceleration of car B and what the graph shows for car A. (d) A braking matatu slows from 20 m/s to 0 in 10 s. Find its acceleration and say what the sign means.
sections.exemplar: (a) Acceleration = change in velocity / time, a = (v - u)/t. From the table, B's velocity goes from u = 20 m/s to v = 30 m/s in t = 5 s, so a = (30 - 20)/5 = 2 m/s^2. (b) Car B's graph is a straight line rising from (0, 20) to (5, 30), then a horizontal line at 30 m/s to t = 7.5 s. Car A's graph is a horizontal line at 20 m/s from 0 to 7.5 s. Axes are labelled t (s) and v (m/s), with 1 cm = 1 s on the x-axis. (c) The gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration: (30 - 20)/5 = 2 m/s^2 for the sloping section of B. A's horizontal line has gradient 0, so car A has zero acceleration and constant velocity. (d) a = (0 - 20)/10 = -2 m/s^2. The negative sign shows deceleration: the matatu is slowing down, and its deceleration is 2 m/s^2.

sections.title: Section 3: How far did each car travel?
sections.prompt: (a) Use the area under B's velocity-time graph, split into a trapezium and a rectangle, to find the distance travelled by car B in 7.5 s. (b) Find the distance travelled by car A in the same time using its graph. (c) Check your answers against the table. (d) How much further did B travel than A, and what does this tell you about the overtake? (e) Car B starts 20 m behind A and ends 20 m ahead of A, and each car is 5 m long. Show how the extra distance B gains fits with these lengths and gaps.
sections.exemplar: (a) Trapezium (0 to 5 s): (20 + 30)/2 x 5 = 125 m. Rectangle (5 to 7.5 s): 30 x 2.5 = 75 m. Total for B = 125 + 75 = 200 m. (b) Car A: rectangle 20 x 7.5 = 150 m. (c) The table gives B = 200 m and A = 150 m at t = 7.5 s, and at t = 5 s B = 125 m, which matches the trapezium. The areas agree with the split-time table. (d) 200 - 150 = 50 m. B travels 50 m more than A because it speeds up at 2 m/s^2 while A stays steady. (e) 50 m = 20 m starting gap + 5 m (length of A) + 5 m (length of B) + 20 m finishing gap. At t = 5 s B has gained 125 - 100 = 25 m, so B's front is level with A's front.

sections.title: Section 4: Why does car A look slow from car B?
sections.prompt: Both speedometers show high readings, yet car A looks slow from car B's point of view. (a) Find the speed of B relative to A once B has reached its final speed, in m/s and in km/h. (b) What was B's speed relative to A at t = 0, and why? (c) Use the B and A distances in the table at t = 4 s and t = 5 s to show that the gap is growing. (d) Find the closing speed of B and oncoming lorry L in m/s and km/h, stating the viewpoint. (e) Use these ideas to explain how two vehicles that are both moving fast can appear to move slowly relative to each other.
sections.exemplar: (a) Same direction, so subtract: B relative to A = 30 - 20 = 10 m/s. 10 x 3.6 = 36 km/h. (b) At t = 0 both cars are at 20 m/s, so B relative to A = 20 - 20 = 0 m/s. It grows to 10 m/s at t = 5 s as B accelerates. (c) At t = 4 s, B minus A = 96 - 80 = 16 m; at t = 5 s, 125 - 100 = 25 m. B gains 9 m in the fifth second, and the gain per second is increasing because B relative to A is increasing. (d) B and L move in opposite directions, so add: 30 + 20 = 50 m/s = 180 km/h. From B's viewpoint, the lorry closes at 50 m/s. (e) Relative speed depends on the viewpoint. When two vehicles go the same way you subtract their speeds, so A looks slow from B (only 10 m/s, 36 km/h, and 0 at the start) even though each speedometer reads high. The oncoming lorry looks very fast from B because speeds add when vehicles move towards each other.

sections.title: Section 5: Final Explanation - Is the overtake safe, and how do we describe and predict it?
sections.prompt: Wanjiru's overtake takes 7.5 s. The lorry L is 500 m ahead of B at t = 0. (a) How far does the lorry travel in 7.5 s? (b) How much road do B and L use together, and how far away is the lorry when B pulls back into lane? (c) Using the closing speed, find the safety margin in seconds. Is the overtake safe? (d) What if the lorry were only 400 m away at t = 0? (e) Write a final answer to the driving question: How can we use distance, time, speed, velocity and graphs to describe and predict how one car overtakes another? Refer to your answers to KICD Questions 1 and 2, graphs, relative speed and the safety decision.
sections.exemplar: (a) Lorry L: 20 m/s x 7.5 s = 150 m. (b) B and L together use 200 + 150 = 350 m. When B is back in lane, the lorry is 500 - 350 = 150 m away. (c) Closing speed is 50 m/s, so margin = 150 / 50 = 3.0 s. A 150 m (3.0 s) margin means the overtake is safe. (d) With the lorry 400 m away: 400 - 350 = 50 m, and 50 / 50 = 1.0 s. This is unsafe because there is very little time to spare. (e) We can describe each vehicle with numbers: velocity = displacement / time gives car A +20 m/s and the lorry -20 m/s (opposite direction), and acceleration a = (v - u)/t gives B 2 m/s^2 as it speeds up from 20 to 30 m/s in 5 s. Velocity-time graphs show these motions: the gradient gives acceleration and the area gives distance (B 200 m, A 150 m, so B gains 50 m in 7.5 s). Relative speed explains what drivers see: B relative to A is only 10 m/s (36 km/h), so A looks slow, while B and L close at 50 m/s (180 km/h). Combining these, B and L need 350 m of road, so with the lorry 500 m away there are 150 m (3.0 s) to spare and the overtake is safe, but with the lorry at 400 m only 1.0 s is left and it is unsafe. So speedometer readings alone do not decide safety; the distances, times and relative speeds do.

rubric.criterion: Velocity and acceleration methods (KICD Questions 1 and 2)
rubric.excellent: States velocity = displacement/time and a = (v - u)/t, explains the vector nature and sign of velocity, converts units correctly and calculates A's +20 m/s, the lorry's -20 m/s, B's 2 m/s^2 and the matatu's -2 m/s^2 with units.
rubric.proficient: Uses both formulas correctly with minor slips in units or in explaining the sign, and gets most values right.
rubric.developing: Confuses speed with velocity or omits conversion, the sign or units, and gets several values wrong.

rubric.excellent: Sketches correct labelled velocity-time graphs for A and B, links gradient to acceleration, and finds B 200 m (125 + 75) and A 150 m from areas, checking against the table.
rubric.proficient: Draws mostly correct graphs and finds the distances with a small error or without checking against the table.
rubric.developing: Graphs are missing labels or shapes are wrong, and the gradient or area is not linked to acceleration or distance.

rubric.excellent: Subtracts for the same direction (10 m/s, 36 km/h) and adds for opposite directions (50 m/s, 180 km/h), states the viewpoint, notes 0 at t = 0 and explains why A looks slow from B.
rubric.proficient: Calculates relative speeds correctly but gives limited explanation or omits the viewpoint or the starting value.
rubric.developing: Adds or subtracts incorrectly, or cannot explain why A looks slow.

rubric.criterion: Safety decision and use of data
rubric.excellent: Correctly finds the lorry's 150 m, the 350 m of road used, the 150 m (3.0 s) margin and the unsafe 50 m (1.0 s) case, and uses table values accurately.
rubric.proficient: Reaches the correct decision with one calculation error or a missing unit or time conversion.
rubric.developing: Decision is not supported by calculations or the numbers are inconsistent with the data.

rubric.criterion: Final Explanation answering the driving question
rubric.excellent: Connects velocity, acceleration, graphs, relative speed and safety in a clear, logical explanation that uses the Naivasha evidence and answers both KICD questions.
rubric.proficient: Answers the driving question using most ideas but with some links missing.
rubric.developing: Lists facts without linking them to the overtake or the driving question.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use distance, time, speed, velocity and graphs to describe and predict how one car overtakes another on a Kenyan road?

lessons.title: Phenomenon: Overtaking on the Naivasha Highway
lessons.observed: What did we observe in the clips? Describe in your own words what car A (blue Toyota Axio), car B (white Subaru) and the oncoming lorry L were doing, and what happened when B returned to its lane.
lessons.learned: What did we notice that puzzled us? Record how the speedometers looked, how car A looked from car B, and what questions we now want to answer about how long, how far and how fast.
lessons.explained: What is our first explanation? Write your best current idea for why car A looks slow from car B even though both speedometers are high, and why the oncoming lorry matters, and say what you still need to find out.

lessons.title: Distance, Displacement, Speed, Velocity and Acceleration: Describing Motion on Kenyan Roads
lessons.observed: Juma's boda boda trip: 4 km distance but 2 km displacement east of the stage. Naivasha Express matatu: 90 km in 1.5 h. Cyclist Atieno: 12 km distance but displacement 0. In the overtaking clip, car A stays steady at 72 km/h, car B speeds up from 72 km/h to 108 km/h, and oncoming lorry L travels the opposite way.
lessons.learned: Distance is total path length (scalar); displacement is straight-line change in position with direction (vector). Speed uses distance; velocity uses displacement and direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity in m/s^2: positive when speeding up, zero for constant velocity, negative (deceleration) when slowing down.
lessons.explained: Car A has constant velocity so zero acceleration. Car B has positive acceleration because its velocity increases. Lorry L has constant negative velocity because it travels towards Naivasha, opposite to the positive direction towards Nakuru, and zero acceleration. A speedometer shows speed only, so velocity is needed to describe direction as well.

lessons.title: Calculating Velocity and Acceleration: How Fast, and How Quickly Does the Speed Change?
lessons.observed: We observed that Car A covers 150 m in 7.5 s, Car B's speedometer rises from 72 km/h to 108 km/h in 5 s and that the oncoming lorry L moves towards Naivasha. We observed that the matatu slows from 20 m/s to 0 in 10 s.
lessons.learned: We learned that velocity = displacement/time and a = (v - u)/t, that km/h is converted to m/s by dividing by 3.6, and that a negative sign shows direction (the lorry, -20 m/s) or deceleration (the braking matatu, a = -2 m/s^2).
lessons.explained: We can explain that A has velocity +20 m/s with zero acceleration, B has acceleration 2 m/s^2 while it speeds up from 20 to 30 m/s, and L has velocity -20 m/s because it travels in the opposite direction, so the numbers describe how each vehicle moves in the overtaking.

lessons.title: Drawing Displacement-Time Graphs: Parked, Steady and Returning Movements
lessons.observed: We observed data for a parked matatu 5 km from Naivasha town, a steady car at 60 km/h with points (0,0), (30,30), (60,60), and cyclist Atieno with points (0,0), (30,6), (40,6), (60,0) in (min, km). We saw that the displacement stays the same, rises steadily, or returns to zero.
lessons.learned: We learned to choose scales, label axes with units, plot points and join them with a ruler to draw displacement-time graphs. A parked vehicle gives a horizontal line, a steady car gives a straight rising line, and a returning cyclist gives a line that rises, goes flat and then falls to zero.
lessons.explained: We can draw a graph of displacement against time for a stationary, steady or returning movement and describe its shape. This helps us describe the steady motion of Car A in the overtaking, and shows we need more tools, such as reading steepness and velocity-time graphs, to describe Car B speeding up.

lessons.title: Interpreting Displacement-Time Graphs: Gradient, Rest and Meeting Points
lessons.observed: We observed that the graph of Atieno's ride has three sections with gradients 12 km/h, 0 and -18 km/h, and that the lines for the matatu leaving Naivasha at 60 km/h and the car leaving Nakuru at 90 km/h cross at 24 min and 24 km from Naivasha.
lessons.learned: We learned that the gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity, that its sign shows direction (negative means the opposite way, like the oncoming lorry L), that a flat line means rest, and that the intersection of two graphs shows where and when two bodies meet.
lessons.explained: We can explain that the vehicles meet when their graphs cross because they are at the same displacement at the same time. This helps us describe the motion of Car A, Car B and the oncoming lorry L, but we still need velocity-time graphs and acceleration to explain how Car B speeds up when overtaking.

lessons.title: Drawing Velocity-Time Graphs: Speeding Up, Steady Speed and Slowing Down
lessons.observed: What did we observe? Example: Car A's velocity-time graph is a horizontal line at 20 m/s. Car B's graph rises in a straight line from 20 m/s at t = 0 to 30 m/s at t = 5 s and then is horizontal until t = 7.5 s. The braking matatu's graph falls in a straight line from 20 m/s at t = 0 to 0 m/s at t = 10 s.
lessons.learned: What did we learn? Example: A rising line shows speeding up (positive acceleration, e.g. 2 m/s^2), a horizontal line shows steady speed (zero acceleration), and a falling line shows slowing down (deceleration, e.g. a = -2 m/s^2). A velocity-time graph has t (s) on the x-axis and v (m/s) on the y-axis.
lessons.explained: How does this help us explain the overtake? Example: The graphs show that Wanjiru in Car B speeds up gradually from 72 km/h to 108 km/h in 5 s and then holds that speed, while Mr Kamau in Car A stays at 72 km/h. Next we need to find how far each car travels and how their speeds compare.

lessons.title: Interpreting Velocity-Time Graphs: Gradient for Acceleration, Area for Distance
lessons.observed: We observed that Car B's velocity-time line slopes upward from 20 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s, then stays flat to 7.5 s; Car A's line is flat at 20 m/s; the braking matatu's line slopes downward from 20 m/s to 0 in 10 s. The areas under the graphs matched the split-time table.
lessons.learned: We learned that the gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration (B: 2 m/s^2; matatu: -2 m/s^2, deceleration 2 m/s^2) and the area under the graph gives distance travelled (B: 125 + 75 = 200 m; A: 150 m; matatu: 100 m).
lessons.explained: We can explain that Car B travels 50 m more than Car A during the overtake because it sped up at 2 m/s^2, and that velocity-time graphs let us describe and predict the motion of the cars on the Naivasha highway using gradient and area.

lessons.title: Relative Speed: Why Does the Overtaken Car Look Slow?
lessons.observed: We observed that at t = 0 both car A and car B show 72 km/h (20 m/s), yet B gains 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 35, 45 and 50 m on A at t = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 7.5 s, and oncoming lorry L moves towards them at 20 m/s.
lessons.learned: We learned that relative speed is found by subtracting speeds for bodies moving in the same direction (B relative to A = 30 - 20 = 10 m/s = 36 km/h, growing from 0 at t = 0 to 10 m/s at t = 5 s) and by adding speeds for bodies moving in opposite directions (B and L: 30 + 20 = 50 m/s = 180 km/h), always stating the viewpoint. The area under B's relative velocity graph, 25 + 25 = 50 m, gives the extra distance B gains.
lessons.explained: Car A looks slow from car B because they move in the same direction, so their relative speed is only 10 m/s (36 km/h) and was 0 at the start, even though both speedometers read high. The oncoming lorry looks very fast from B because it closes at 50 m/s (180 km/h), which is why the overtake needs careful checking in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Applying Linear Motion: Is Wanjiru's Overtake Safe?
lessons.observed: What we observed: In the Naivasha clip, overtaking car B took 7.5 s to pass overtaken car A. In that time B travelled 200 m, A travelled 150 m and oncoming lorry L travelled 150 m. B gained 50 m on A.
lessons.learned: What we learned: We can combine acceleration (a = 2 m/s^2), areas under velocity-time graphs and relative speed to decide if an overtake is safe. B and L together use 350 m of road. The safety margin is the distance to the lorry minus 350 m, and dividing by the closing speed of 50 m/s gives the margin in seconds.
lessons.explained: How this explains the phenomenon: With the lorry 500 m away, the margin is 150 m, or 3.0 s, so Wanjiru's overtake is safe. If the lorry were only 400 m away, the margin would be 50 m, or 1.0 s, which is unsafe. Both cars can have high speedometer readings, but safety depends on relative speeds and the road available, not on speedometer readings alone.

lessons.title: Final Model and Answer to the Driving Question: Overtaking on the Naivasha Highway
lessons.observed: We observed Car B (white Subaru) overtake Car A (blue Toyota Axio) near Naivasha: both start at 72 km/h (20 m/s), B speeds up to 108 km/h (30 m/s) in 5 s and is back in lane at 7.5 s, while the oncoming lorry L approaches at 20 m/s.
lessons.learned: We learned that velocity = displacement/time and a = (v - u)/t; that the gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration (2 m/s^2) and the area gives distance (B 200 m, A 150 m); and that relative speed is the difference of speeds in the same direction (10 m/s) and the sum in opposite directions (50 m/s).
lessons.explained: We explained that A looks slow from B because B relative to A is only 10 m/s (36 km/h), and that the overtake is safe because B and L need 350 m of road, leaving 150 m (3.0 s) of the 500 m; with the lorry at 400 m the margin is only 1.0 s, which is unsafe.
